arxiv:2611.17186: Federated learning (FL) enables independent data owners to train models collaboratively without centralizing raw data. However, identifying collaborators, preparing training tasks, and coordinating execution and incentives hinder its practical adoption by organizations without specialized expertise. We present Cortex-FL, an agent-native FL system that enables users to express learning objectives in natural language and delegate the collaboration required to train a model. Agents translate these objectives into shared tasks, discover collaborators, and negotiate participation agreements, connecting collaboration formation with distributed training and incentive management. The architecture separates agent coordination from local execution authority, allowing owners to delegate coordination while retaining control over their data, computation, and financial commitments. We demonstrate the complete workflow on a four-node deployment, in which a model requested in natural language proceeds through collaboration formation, contract-governed training, verified model delivery, and x402 settlement on a blockchain testnet.
arxiv:2611.17129: Federated learning experiments can produce reasonable-looking results even when the experiment implementation differs from the intended experimental protocol. Small errors in configuration, data partitioning, aggregation, randomness, evaluation, or checkpoint recovery may therefore affect a comparison without causing the program to fail. We present FedBrew, a research codebase for controlled and reproducible federated learning experiments. Its focus is controlled simulation with checks of specified conditions of the intended experimental protocol. FedBrew uses configuration checks, identifiable client data partitions, checkpoint recovery checks, self-describing run records, and development-time checks of scientific conditions. These checks assess, for example, whether client partitions are disjoint and exhaustive and aggregation weights match the prescribed rule; numerical and recovery checks examine non-finite client model states and interrupted runs. The same structure also provides clear extension points and automated checks for new algorithms, datasets, models, and tasks, whether they are added by researchers or AI coding agents. FedBrew therefore supports reproducible and inspectable FL experiments through checks of specified software and scientific conditions and the run records associated with reported results.
arxiv:2611.16856: Federated Learning (FL) with Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) enables efficient adaptation of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet its energy and carbon costs across hardware remain poorly understood. We evaluated federated Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning on NVIDIA A40, RTX 6000 Ada, and A100 GPUs using a $2^2$ full factorial design with 135M/360M models and 10/100 local steps. CodeCarbon tracked energy and estimated CO$_2$-equivalent emissions. Descriptive allocation of variation assigned 84.8-91.2% of energy and emissions variation to local steps within these ranges. On A40 and RTX 6000 Ada, configurations with fewer steps achieved comparable accuracy with roughly 6-8-fold lower energy consumption and higher accuracy per kWh. These findings support smaller local budgets for energy-efficient federated fine-tuning within the evaluated setting.
arxiv:2611.16772: Federated learning over distributed intrusion-detection sensors naturally produces \emph{class-concentrated} non-IID data, where an entire attack class is held by a single client and absent elsewhere. We show this collapses federated averaging in a specific, localized way: the output layer holds one decision boundary per class, and when a class's aggregation weight comes overwhelmingly from clients that have never seen it, its neuron receives an active anti-signal rather than mere dilution, collapsing to zero. On CIC-DDoS2019, standard FedAvg drives the concentrated LDAP class to $0.00 \pm 0.00\%$ F1 across every seed. We propose Class-Competence Aggregation (CCA), which aggregates the output layer per class using each client's own locally reported validation F1 as the weight, while hidden layers remain under standard size-weighted FedAvg. CCA requires no server-held auxiliary data and adds only one F1 scalar per class per round beyond the feature-scaling and class-count exchanges common to any federated pipeline. On our primary CNN-LSTM architecture, CCA alone raises LDAP F1 from $0\%$ to $84.83 \pm 1.65\%$, and the full method reaches $91.64 \pm 0.57\%$ macro F1, closing the federated-to-centralized gap from $-42.53$ to $-4.05$ points. Benchmarked against four other federated methods under identical partitions and seeds, CCA is the only one that recovers the concentrated class substantially and reliably; a $178\times$ smaller MLP shows the same qualitative recovery, though less completely, confirming the effect holds across architecture scale even as its magnitude varies. Results are validated across three seeds and replicated on a second dataset, CICIDS2017.
arxiv:2611.16065: Federated learning (FL) systems increasingly rely on blockchain based reward mechanisms to incentivize participation while preserving data privacy. We design and empirically evaluate two complementary Solidity smart contracts for FL reward distribution: the first one that allocates rewards proportionally to a publicly disclosed quality score, and a privacy preserving variant that hides individual quality scores behind a zero-knowledge (ZK) proof of a threshold condition. Both contracts mint a non transferable, use-and-burn token maintaining a trustless incentive structure. We evaluate the two designs through MNIST training with adversarial behavior, including Sybil attacks, zero gradient and random noise, across three independent random seeds. Our results reveal a fundamental tradeoff between cryptographic privacy and incentive fairness. The privacy preserving architecture strictly degrades system robustness, doubling the adversary's average reward capture while introducing severe outcome variance. This vulnerability is driven by a structural self-inclusion bias within cosine-similarity scoring: as the global model converges, legitimate gradient updates naturally diminish, rendering them statistically indistinguishable from bounded noise. Adversaries exploit this dynamic to systematically breach the ZK threshold, triggering a late stage failure cascade that culminates in absolute adversary monopoly over the reward pool and the total exclusion of honest contributors. Alongside a closed-form theorem formalizing this privacy--Sybil resistance tradeoff, we map strict mainnet deployment boundaries via linear gas scaling models, explicitly incorporating the post-Fusaka EIP-7825 per transaction gas cap. Ultimately, while cryptographically secure, static threshold ZK gates fail as incentive layer fairness mechanisms under realistic FL convergence dynamics on standard benchmarks.
arxiv:2611.15917: Organisations that apply the same published decision rule often hold private evidence that the rule is wrong for their own cases, and will not pool it. We describe a learning mechanism for that setting whose unit of change is an owned edit. The published rule is compiled exactly into a small ReLU network, a structured prior. Each party's learner searches a small typed space of declarations, a few named values such as subject, scope, form and size, and proposes one only when its own records pass a selection-aware evidence gate. The learning is that gated search around the prior. In two analyses registered before they ran, on synthetic data with 20 sampled hidden truths, the learner at 30 records per party was non-inferior, within 2 points, to all seven tuned baselines (a confined gradient learner, Ditto, FedRep, federated averaging, two pooled networks and pooled gradient-boosted trees), scoring 96.6% against 91.7% for the unchanged rule; the same search without the prior or the gate scored 84.0%. In a third registered test, typed edits over a network trained on shared records beat that network alone by 5.4 points and the same edits over the published rule by 3.1. An acceptance body recomputes each edit from its declaration and writes it into units reserved for that party, so by construction an edit changes no decision about any other subject, withdraws exactly, discloses at most log2 of the typed space's size in bits, and can hide nothing beyond its declared values. We report where it loses: truths shared by all parties, relaxations, ten records, a pre-stated gate criterion that failed in both runs, and a language model given the records that decided about as accurately on one draw. On a rule-only base, a table of owned exceptions makes the same decisions.
arxiv:2611.15707: Federated Bayesian Optimization (FedBO) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for enhancing Bayesian Optimization (BO) in distributed, privacy-sensitive settings, enabling agents to accelerate the optimization of their local objectives by sharing knowledge about their similarities without exposing raw data. However, existing methods rely on restrictive assumptions, such as near-identical objective functions or shared Gaussian process hyperparameters that are often violated in heterogeneous real-world applications. We present GLOBAFED, a novel framework that enables efficient knowledge transfer across different but related objectives without compromising privacy. At its core is a probabilistic neural network surrogate with a shared feature-extracting backbone and agent-specific heads equipped with varia- tional Bayesian last layers to provide uncertainty estimates. During optimization, agents use federated learning on the shared backbone to collaboratively build a common latent feature representation, while agent-specific heads adapt to their individual objectives. Our empirical results demonstrate that GLOBAFED significantly accelerates convergence and reaches better final performance compared to state-of-the-art FedBO baselines, and enables agents to warm-start their optimization from previously learned global features.
arxiv:2611.15499: Model broadcast in federated learning (FL) with wireless channels faces significant challenges due to large model sizes and heterogeneous, unreliable channel conditions. While rateless coding has been widely adopted in modern broadcast communications to handle channel heterogeneity, its potential for model broadcast in FL remains largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we propose a joint source-channel coding scheme based on rateless coding to improve the robustness and efficiency of downlink model broadcast in FL. Specifically, we establish a rigorous convergence analysis of FL to inform the rateless code and quantization design under noisy downlink channel conditions. Moreover, by observing that the iterative process of FL naturally provides prior information about client updates, we leverage client-side local models as conditional prior information to aid the decoding process, thereby reducing transmission costs. Extensive simulations demonstrate that our rateless coding scheme significantly enhances downlink model broadcast efficiency in FL, while retaining comparable training accuracies for both homogeneous and heterogeneous data distributions.
arxiv:2611.15165: Federated learning combines complementary knowledge across clients to alleviate local data limitations without sharing raw samples. However, data heterogeneity can cause conflicting updates and hinder generalization. Update coordination reduces interference among client updates, while flatness optimization reduces sensitivity to parameter perturbations to improve generalization. Existing joint designs largely target specific algorithms, limiting flexible combinations of these approaches. To address this problem, we propose a unified federated learning framework that bridges update coordination and flatness optimization. Clients separately accumulate descent signals and flatness corrections along the same local trajectory. The server coordinates both groups with independent states before fusing their outputs into a global update. Explicit conversion between trajectory signals and model updates enables different coordination strategies to work with compatible local or globally guided flatness mechanisms without changing the inference architecture. Experiments show that the evaluated combinations generally improve average and worst-client accuracy over update coordination alone, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed framework in combining these complementary optimization mechanisms.
arxiv:2611.15025: Federated learning often assumes that data is fixed in advance, which is unrealistic in many real-world scenarios where new data continuously arrives, causing catastrophic forgetting. To address this challenge, we propose FCLPF (Federated Class Incremental Learning with Pseudo Features), a method that uses pseudo features generated from prototypes to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. Our approach reduces communication costs and improves efficiency by eliminating the need for past data and avoiding computationally heavy models like GANs. Experimental results on CIFAR-100 show that FCLPF achieves an average accuracy of 51.87% and an average forgetting of 9.62%, significantly outperforming existing baselines with an average accuracy of 47.72% and forgetting of 20.46%. On TinyImageNet, FCLPF achieves 37.56% accuracy and 3.14% forgetting, compared to the baselines' 27.69% accuracy and 24.46% forgetting, demonstrating the superior performance of FCLPF.
arxiv:2611.14272: Objective: Epidemic outbreaks are often asynchronous across regions, yet collaborative forecasting is hampered by privacy laws and heterogeneous public health interventions. We developed and evaluated, as a proof of concept, a federated learning (FL) framework for cross-regional COVID-19 forecasting under asynchronous outbreaks among Guangdong, Macau, and Portugal, while maintaining data sovereignty. Methods: Using daily case data from WHO and China CDC for the three regions, whose outbreaks were asynchronous and interventions heterogeneous, we trained Long Short-Term Memory networks via FL for short-term forecasting, benchmarked against localized and centralized training using Root Mean Square Error, Mean Absolute Error, and Symmetric Mean Absolute Percentage Error. All experiments used the Flower FL framework with consistent hyperparameters across sites. Publicly available, aggregated case-count data were used so that the centralized benchmark could be computed as a reference. Results: The dataset comprised 1,233 daily observations (411 days) of new confirmed COVID-19 cases from November 24, 2021, to January 8, 2023. The earlier Omicron wave in Portugal supplied transmission dynamics that improved forecasts in the later-onset regions of Macau and Guangdong. The FL model achieved a normalized Root Mean Square Error of 0.028, an 88.3% improvement over the local model (0.240) and comparable to the centralized model, with network overhead mainly determined by model size and aggregation rounds. Conclusion: FL achieved short-term forecasting accuracy close to centralized training while maintaining data residency, with acceptable overhead. Leveraging asynchronous outbreaks across regions may offer a practical path to privacy-preserving collaborative forecasting, though prospective validation is required.
arxiv:2611.13987: Wireless federated learning (FL) suffers from two coupled bottlenecks: statistical heterogeneity across clients and communication-constrained model synchronization over unreliable wireless links. Instead of focusing on algorithmic design and/or wireless resource optimization, this paper provides a systematic study of pinching antenna (PA)-empowered FL for heterogeneous wireless networks and develops a unified communication-and-learning framework. Specifically, we integrate a segmented waveguide-enabled pinching antenna (SWAN) architecture with a heterogeneity-robust FL algorithm based on client variance reduction and dual quantization, so as to jointly mitigate communication bottlenecks and client drift. On this basis, we further develop a two-stage SWAN-assisted downlink protocol and formulate fairness-oriented uplink optimization problems for PA positioning, bandwidth allocation, and quantization design. Efficient solution frameworks are then derived for the resulting downlink and uplink optimization problems. Experimental results show the superiority of the proposed design in convergence speed and final accuracy under non-independent and identically distributed data and communication bottlenecks.
arxiv:2611.13976: Federated learning enables multiple clients to collaboratively train a machine-learning model without directly sharing their local datasets. However, as prior works have shown, the gradients exchanged during training may reveal sensitive information about client data. Most existing attacks usually optimize dummy inputs to match the true client gradients (Gradient Inversion Attacks), while some attempt to reconstruct them based on the observation that aggregate gradients from a fully connected (FC) layer are a linear combination of its inputs. In this work, we extend this observation by showing that aggregate gradients from an FC layer with the correct scaling are actually an affine combination of its inputs. We evaluate a gradient inversion attack that leverages either known linear-subspace information or its affine-subspace counterpart at each FC layer to improve reconstruction accuracy. Our results show that subspace-based methods can substantially improve reconstruction quality over the chosen baselines in certain settings. We further demonstrate that moderate overestimation of the batch size can generally improve or preserve reconstruction quality, even when the true batch size is unknown. We additionally examine reconstruction under gradient perturbations introduced by a differential privacy (DP) mechanism, providing insight into the effectiveness of the considered formulations under noisy conditions.
arxiv:2611.13708: Conventional federated learning relies on the shared model backbone to aggregate client updates, limiting collaboration among institutions that deploy large language models (LLMs) from different families and at different scales. We propose Federated Verifier Pool (FEDVP), a new federated learning paradigm that enables heterogeneous clients to collaborate through shared verification rather than parameter aggregation. Each client trains a verifier using local data and responses generated by its chosen LLM backbone. The server pools these independently trained verifiers and combines their judgments to select answers without merging model parameters. This allows both LLM backbones and verifiers to differ in architecture and size, while keeping the LLM backbones frozen and deriving collaborative gains from improved answer selection. We evaluate FEDVP across five public medical question-answering datasets treated as federated clients, using Qwen and LLaMA backbones ranging from 3B to 14B parameters. FEDVP consistently improves performance across all five clients and outperforms the strongest conventional federated baselines by 1.46-5.79 percentage points in mean accuracy.
arxiv:2611.13491: Detecting backdoor attacks in federated learning (FL) is challenging because malicious clients can manipulate the global model while preserving main-task performance. Static model-update statistics may therefore fail to clearly distinguish malicious from benign clients. Unlearning-based detectors instead probe client models through loss ascent on clean server data, but detection performance degrades with scarce proxy data. We propose Screening via Unlearning Response Analysis (SURA), a data-efficient detector. SURA reuses the same small clean proxy across multiple train-mode loss-ascent steps, strengthening client responses without additional clean data. For federated vision models with batch normalization (BN), repeated probing also changes BN running statistics and can confound endpoint measurements. SURA addresses this by restoring the shared pre-probe BN state only at readout while preserving the parameter changes induced by probing. This separates repeated probing from response measurement and removes BN drift and the interaction between parameter and BN-state changes from the readout. Across six backdoor attacks, SURA uses only 10 clean server images, outperforms methods under the same data budget, and approaches the robustness obtained with much larger proxy sets.
10.1145/3815789.3827953: In federated learning (FL), data providers jointly train a machine learning model without sharing training data. This makes it challenging to provide verifiable claims about the trained model, e.g., related to the employed training data, data sanitization, or training algorithm—a malicious data provider can simply deviate from the correct training protocol without detection. Prior FL training systems have used trusted execution environments (TEEs) to protect the training computation, relying on the confidentiality and integrity of TEEs. TEE confidentiality, however, has been shown to be vulnerable to various attacks, e.g., via side channels. We describe ExclaveFL , a system for training FL models that establishes verifiable claims about models through fine-grained runtime attestation proofs. Since such proofs only require integrity, ExclaveFL generates them using exclaves , which are integrity-only execution environments without software-managed secrets, making them immune to data leakage attacks. ExclaveFL uses exclaves to attest data transformations during FL training, and the runtime attestation proofs then form an attested dataflow graph of the entire training computation. The graph is checked by an auditor to ensure that the trained model satisfies claims, e.g., about the use of data sanitization by data providers or aggregation by the model provider. Since exclaves require minor yet proprietary firmware changes, we evaluate a variant with similar performance but slightly weaker security guarantees on existing AMD SEV-SNP hardware. We show that ExclaveFL introduces less than 12% overhead compared to unprotected FL model training.
10.67728/eci.2026.003: **A Communication-Aware Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework for UAV-Swarm Relay Deployment via 3D Trajectory Control** **Shanshan He** Department of Communication Engineering, Jilin University, Changchun 130012, China **Abstract:** Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms can restore communication after infrastructure failure and extend low-altitude Internet of Things (IoT) services, but trajectory decisions interact with access links, backhaul bottlenecks, data queues, battery use, service fairness, and flight constraints. This paper formulates these couplings as a communication-aware constrained Markov game and implements a lightweight communication-aware multi-agent dueling double DQN (CA-MAD3QN). The implemented learner controls only discrete three-dimensional UAV motion; user association, bandwidth, access power, and the MEC term are fixed or rule based and are not claimed as learned optimization variables. Backhaul capacity is propagated to every user through an explicit service-scaling factor before queue evolution. The revised numerical study compares CA-MAD3QN with discrete MAPPO, vanilla DQN, one-step mod-el-predictive optimization, greedy tracking, and static deployment over three independent training seeds and reports 95% confidence intervals. Under the stress setting, CA-MAD3QN achieves an episode utility of 85.36 ± 28.94 (95% CI); the evidence does not establish universal superiority over the competitive baselines, so no such claim is made. In the two-UAV testbed, an exact joint-action projection eliminates modeled realized violations; disabling that projection for the same trained policy yields 0.863 violations per slot on average. Preliminary small-scale tests with two to four UAVs show increasing aggregate throughput but also expose projection and training-variance limitations. The results are therefore pre-sented as an auditable proof of concept rather than hardware validation. **Keywords:** UAV Swarm; Communication Relay; Three-Dimensional Trajectory Optimization; Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning; Mobile Edge Computing; Safety Projection; Federated Learning **Citation:** He S. A Communication-Aware Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework for UAV-Swarm Relay Deployment via 3D Trajectory Control. Engineering and Computing Insights. Published online November 10, 2026:22-35. doi:10.67728/eci.2026.003
10.1145/3815789.3827948: Federated Learning (FL) enables multiple devices to collaboratively train a global model while preserving data privacy. However, the substantial memory requirements during local training pose a significant challenge for deploying FL on resource-constrained mobile devices in real-world scenarios. This paper introduces FedRD, a memory-efficient FL framework that well trades off model performance and training efficiency through hierarchical management. Specifically, FedRD features the following core techniques. First, a Memory Budget Predictor is designed to well estimate the available memory under fluctuating workloads in highly dynamic environments. With the memory budget, a Memory-aware Participant Selector is designed to select the participating devices for each training round through jointly evaluating the memory, computation, and statistical utility in order to well balance the model performance and training efficiency. Finally, we develop a memory-efficient training engine that enables local training under strict memory budgets by reshaping allocation workloads from both spatial and temporal perspectives, effectively mitigating memory fragmentation. Extensive experiments are conducted to evaluate FedRD on both simulation testbed and off-the-shelf mobile devices. The experiment results demonstrate that FedRD significantly outperforms the baselines, achieving up to 41% higher model accuracy while reducing wall-clock time by 9 × across varying memory budgets.
arxiv:2611.14239: In this paper, we study the convergence of Federated Averaging (FedAvg) with partial participation under a general variance condition. In each communication round, the server samples $S$ of the $n$ clients uniformly at random without replacement. The stochastic gradients are assumed to satisfy the so-called ABC condition, which allows their variance to grow with the local objective gaps. For smooth nonconvex objectives, we establish a finite-time stationarity bound in terms of the heterogeneity measure $σ_f^\star:=f^\star-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i^\star$ and the client sampling factor $I_S:=(n-S)/(n-1)$. Here, $f^\star$ and $f_i^\star$ denote the infima of the global average objective and client $i$'s local objective, respectively. The bound exhibits a linear speedup in the number of sampled clients $S$ and recovers the full-participation result when $S=n$. Under diminishing stepsizes, we further prove that the gradient norm converges to zero both in expectation and almost surely. Notably, compared with existing analyses of FedAvg with partial participation, our results require no additional data heterogeneity assumption such as bounded gradient dissimilarity (BGD), and the sampling-induced term in our bound is not amplified by the number of local updates at the leading order. The importance of removing the BGD assumption is illustrated by an example that is smooth and lower bounded but violates BGD, yet is covered by our analysis.
arxiv:2611.14590: Classification of lung adenocarcinoma into poorly differentiated (PD) and well-to-moderately differentiated (WMD) subtypes plays an important role in patient survival; however, consistent classification is difficult due to inter-observer variability among pathologists. Collecting data from multiple hospitals is also challenging due to patient privacy concerns. This study proposes a web-based federated learning system that shares only locally trained model weights without sharing patient data between institutions. The UNI2 foundation model and CLAM-SB were used to classify pathological whole slide images. A four-client federated learning system was constructed, and the NLST cohort was reserved exclusively for external validation. In centralized evaluation, joint training with CPTAC and TCGA outperformed single-institution training on external validation, confirming the necessity of multi-institutional data integration. FedAvg, FedProx, FedBN, and FedNova were compared as federated learning algorithms under identical experimental conditions. Test AUC ranked as FedBN, FedProx, FedNova, and FedAvg. FedNova showed the most balanced classification performance between PD and WMD. L1-norm structural pruning at 20%, 30%, and 40% sparsity was applied to reduce model transmission size. FedAvg, FedProx, and FedBN showed a tendency of decreasing Test AUC under pruning, while FedNova achieved improved Test AUC across all sparsity levels. A web-based application was developed supporting slide upload, local training, AI classification, and attention heatmap-based visualization. The combination of FedNova and 40% pruning was confirmed as a practical approach that improves communication efficiency and classification performance while protecting patient privacy.
arxiv:2611.12131: One-shot Federated Graph Learning (OFGL) has emerged as a communication-efficient paradigm for federated graph learning under strict bandwidth constraints, compressing collaboration into a single transmission round. Nevertheless, this extreme setting suffers from a fundamental Single-Transmission Bottleneck, which limits both the quality and utility of exchanged knowledge. First, while existing methods attempt to distill private graphs into shareable proxies, their aggressive one-shot compression inherently triggers a fidelity crisis. This compression distorts local graph topology and semantics across clients, leading to externalized knowledge underexpression. Second, although the server aggregates these proxies to update global models, current integration schemes suffer from transferability agnosticism. The server cannot reliably identify cross-client collaboration potential, thus resulting in integrated knowledge underutilization. To tackle these dual challenges, we propose FedHFT, an effective One-Shot Personalized Federated Graph Learning (OPFGL) framework that addresses this bottleneck from two perspectives, namely High-Fidelity Knowledge Externalization and Transferability-Ware Knowledge Integration. We use Fidelity-Driven Proxy Refinement to preserve client-side knowledge fidelity, and Transferability-Steered Personalized Collaboration to enable adaptive server-side collaboration. The superiority of FedHFT is validated through extensive experiments on both homophilic and heterophilic graphs. The code is available at https://github.com/Jumpy-Juice/FedHFT.
arxiv:2611.13331: Fine-tuning large-scale foundation models across resource-constrained, distributed clients presents significant computational and communication challenges. While merging Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) with Federated Learning (FL) enables rank-based flexibility, the interdependence of the adaptation matrices ($\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$) often complicates optimization. In this work, we theoretically demonstrate that LoRA fine-tuning with Gaussian initialization and a frozen $\mathbf{A}$ matrix acts as a stochastic approximation of full fine-tuning, where batch gradients are subject to a random, rank-dependent perturbation. Motivated by this insight, we propose freezing and periodically resampling $\mathbf{A}$ matrices at the client level. This strategy decouples the $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ gradients, diminishes LoRA low-rank constraints and reduces both computational and uplink communication overheads by 50\%, allowing for the reallocation of resources toward higher adaptation ranks. Furthermore, we show that in this frozen-$\mathbf{A}$ regime, the adaptation rank $r$ directly governs the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the perturbed gradients. Specifically, we find that the SNR increases linearly with $r$, implying that clients' learning rates must be dynamically scaled with their adaptation ranks for higher utility. Building on these foundations, we introduce SPRA-LoRA (Stochastic Projection Rank-Aware LoRA), a federated rank-aware fine-tuning strategy that utilizes frozen, resampled $\mathbf{A}$ matrices and rank-dependent learning rates for clients. We also prove its convergence with heterogeneous client resources. Our experiments across benchmark datasets demonstrate that SPRA-LoRA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines with half the overhead on clients.
arxiv:2611.13137: Optimization methods, including the Muon optimizer based on the Linear Minimization Oracle (LMO) and momentum orthogonalization, have shown strong empirical performance in large-scale and distributed learning, yet their robustness to adversarial behavior and data heterogeneity is not well understood. We study these methods within a unified first-order trust-region framework and analyze Muon-based updates with robust aggregation for Byzantine-robust distributed and federated learning. Our analysis does not rely on the i.i.d. assumption and introduces a non-Euclidean notion of heterogeneity consistent with the trust-region geometry. Under this framework, we establish convergence guarantees for both general non-convex and star-convex objectives. Our results provide a theoretical characterization of Byzantine-robust Muon-based optimization, with an additive heterogeneity error floor consistent with known impossibility results, under explicit aggregation assumptions. Under an explicit additive oracle-error condition, the guarantees also cover inexact orthogonalization, with the non-convex Byzantine terms in the bound's numerator unchanged but a smaller progress denominator. In simulated federated training with ResNet-18 and ViT-Tiny on CIFAR-10, additional image benchmarks, and a 38M-parameter byte-level language model on TinyStories, the tested Muon configuration attains higher attacked accuracy (lower perplexity) than the tested SGD and normalized-SGD configurations, and than sign updates on CIFAR-10. Fixed-honest controls further show a substantial RFA advantage over averaging under a bounded RFA-query attack, higher attacked accuracy for Muon-NS than tensorwise Euclidean normalization from shared checkpoints, and lower held-out TinyStories perplexity than a tuned AdamW baseline.
arxiv:2611.12187: Federated learning (FL) is a promising research paradigm that enables collaborative model training across distributed clients without data sharing. To handle unlabeled data in local clients, existing unsupervised FL research has primarily focused on tasks like clustering and self-supervised representation learning, leaving the critical problem of unsupervised visual recognition largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce FedUR, the first framework designed for unsupervised recognition by leveraging the zero-shot capabilities of pre-trained vision-language models like CLIP. Specifically, FedUR addresses data heterogeneity through a pseudo-labeling mechanism with a class-aware data selection strategy. This strategy first estimates a global pseudo-label distribution, then allocates pseudo-labeled data to clients accordingly. To handle the uncertainty of conventional positive pseudo-labels, FedUR further incorporates class weights and a negative pseudo-labeling strategy. Furthermore, FedUR proposes a personalized prompt aggregation protocol where general visual prompts are aggregated on the server, and personalized text prompts encoding local knowledge are retained on clients. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedUR consistently outperforms baseline methods under both label-level and feature-level distribution shifts. We believe this work paves the way for further advances in federated unsupervised recognition. Code will be available at {github.com/tim-learn/FedUR/}}.
arxiv:2611.11774: Distributed artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly relies on wireless networks, where communication and computing resources shape how AI tasks are configured and executed. However, resource availability alone does not determine how effectively these tasks can be supported, since different information selections and transmission strategies may yield different AI performance under the same resource constraints. To address this challenge, this article presents Wireless AI Networks as a unified design perspective for bidirectional adaptation between wireless communication and distributed intelligence. Specifically, an AI-executable resource budget characterizes candidate AI configurations, while task-level information value guides their selection and wireless resource allocation. Building on these principles, a wireless-AI co-adaptation framework coordinates resource abstraction, joint configuration and allocation, and execution feedback. Two complementary experiments illustrate this perspective: update selection and statistical correction improve federated learning under identical model-update payload budgets, while sensitivity-aware power allocation reduces model accuracy degradation under the same average transmit-power constraint. Together, these results highlight the importance of coordinating resource feasibility and task-level information value in distributed AI execution.
arxiv:2611.11744: This work proposes the Adaptive Federated Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (AFHMC) for Bayesian federated learning (FL) tasks. The prior work on HMC applications for FL achieves $O(\sqrt{d}/ε)$ communication cost under log-convex distributions, already demonstrating its advantage over the Langevin dynamic-based counterpart. Based on a refined analysis, this paper further reveals the benefit of HMC for the FL regime by incorporating a control mechanism for local node shifts. We prove that AFHMC at most requires $O(\{d/ε^2\}^{1/3})$ communication cost up to a logarithmic term, which is significantly better than the existing results. Moreover, the proposed method adapts to client heterogeneity. Under low-heterogeneity settings (i.e., the target sampling precision $ε^2$ is higher than the heterogeneity level), the communication rate of AFHMC can be as good as $O(\log(d/ε^2))$, resembling the communication costs for FL optimization tools. To the best of our knowledge, this provides the first logarithmic communication complexity result for federated sampling, even though it requires low heterogeneity. Numerically, we also justify AFHMC's advantage under the low-heterogeneity regime. Our code is available at https://github.com/laaaarrywang/Adaptive-Federated-HMC
10.15587/978-617-8360-29-0: The monograph aims to provide a detailed analysis of current biometric authentication technologies using electrocardiographic (ECG) signals and voice as two fundamentally different but complementary modalities. The relevance of the work is due to the ongoing and evolving crisis of password-based security mechanisms (annual leaks affecting billions of user accounts, and generative speech synthesis technologies moving towards levels where the human voice can be imitated in a matter of minutes). The combination of ECG (an innate marker of life that is almost impossible to fake) with voice (which provides simple contactless verification at a distance) forms a logical and specialized premise for a new generation of biometric structures. The first part is devoted to the basic theory of biometric technologies: nine principles (uniqueness, stability, measurability, universality, resistance to counterfeiting, security, accuracy, standardization and acceptability) for building systems; a comparative analysis of nine physiological and behavioral modalities; nine functional modules of a typical biometric system; architectural solutions from autonomous to cloud-based and adaptive with Zero Trust support; a system of quality assessment metrics – FAR/FRR/EER/DET/minDCF curves – and approaches to ensuring demographic equity. The second part is devoted exclusively to ECG-based biometrics. The unique characteristics of the electrocardiographic signal, arising from anatomical, electrophysiological and neurohumoral factors, are further explained in physiological terms. All processing stages are described – from signal acquisition (with contact and non-contact methods), noise filtering (adaptive LMS filter or 1D U-Net based on neural networks), cardiac cycle segmentation using the Pan–Tompkins algorithm, autoencoder architectures, formation of morphological, temporal and spectral features for average heart beat analysis and dimensionality reduction based on PCA/LDA – up to classification and decision making. Comparison of two-class SVM, k-NN, decision trees and neural networks in different configurations was performed using four datasets (MIT-BIH, PTB, Fantasia, Lviv Biometric Data Set). The highest identification accuracy (98.90%, FAR 0.18·10⁻³, FRR 7.32·10⁻³) was achieved by a neural network with a hidden layer architecture (256, 128). It was experimented with deep embedding architectures (1D-ResNet, Transformer) as well as metric loss functions (Triplet Loss, ArcFace) and tested whether it is possible to deploy it on edge devices. The third section contains the full voice biometric chain: classical MFCC, LPC and PNCC descriptors, speech preprocessing methods (spectral subtraction, Wiener filtering, VAD and neural network optimization using Wave-U-Net), and finally four modern neural network architectures for speaker embedding-ECAPA-TDNN/WavLM/TitaNet/PyAnnote. In the framework of the experimental study, it is shown that TitaNet achieves the highest verification accuracy (0.96), and ECAPA-TDNN – 0.95 and scales better with increasing number of users; while WavLM, under difficult conditions, demonstrates the highest sensitivity to channel variations. The fourth section covers several practical implementation topics: international legal regulation (GDPR, AI Act, BIPA, ISO/IEC 24745 and 30107 standards), ethical aspects of the use of biometric data, architectural solutions for industrial implementation (design of a template database with approximate search algorithms: HNSW and IVF-PQ; cancelable biometric methods; fault tolerance; integration of BioAPI and FIDO2), implementation scenarios in the e-ID industry: banking, telecommunications, medicine, public administration and corporate security; the topic of the user interface - from ease of use to accessibility and economic analysis of costs against return on investment. Strategic development opportunities are identified: multimodal integration of ECG and voice at the level of feature fusion, scoring and decision-making; adaptive systems based on federated learning with differentiated privacy against threats from generative AI; transfer to decentralized identification based on Zero-Knowledge Proof. The scientific novelty of the work is determined by a new integrated concept of biometric authentication with a combination of ECG and voice; a comparative study of modern embedding architectures not only with an assessment of accuracy, but also with a determination of the scalability of models and resistance to spoofing attacks, based on the most modern generative models; as well as a quantitative measurement of how serious a threat these models pose to voice biometrics systems. The practical significance depends on the ability to directly apply the results to build biometric systems in finance, telecommunications, medicine and other areas of social activity. The monograph is designed for researchers, graduate students and students of specialties in information security, digital signal processing and machine learning, as well as for practicing specialists in the field of design and implementation of biometric authentication systems.
10.48550/arxiv.2611.11866: Submodular maximization seeks a small subset best representing a large dataset. In its federated setting, the server is a single point of failure and some clients may be Byzantine. Removing the server raises a trilemma of decentraliza- tion, efficiency, and security. We propose DeFSM, a Byzantine-robust and communication-efficient architecture that replaces the server with a lightweight smart contract and a pool of independent, consensus-free agents. Its aggregation rule, SafeGM, builds on two notions from combinatorial geometry: Tukey depth and safe points (the points lying in the convex hull of the good points wherever the bad points are). SafeGM makes the robust decision on 2D Gaussian random projections, which the contract can compute efficiently, and lifts it back as a convex combination of actual updates. Since lifting loses information, it uses the projected geometric median only when its depth certifies it, and otherwise a Tukey median. The share of bad updates is then bounded only by a count: how many there are, not what they contain. We prove, and confirm empirically, that this bound controls the solution quality. On CIFAR10 and PathMNIST, with up to 30% Byzantine clients and agents, DeFSM never collapses and retains on average about 91% of the quality of the ideal reference, the geometric median at a trusted central server. The geometric median decentralized in its best setting would retain about 96%, but the contract cannot compute it, and so each agent would have to download six times more data, or each client twice as much.
10.48550/arxiv.2611.12604: AI safety evaluations often involve sensitive prompts and proprietary models. Evaluators want to keep their evaluation prompts secret from model owners to prevent purposeful or incidental data leakage, ensuring longer usefulness of their benchmark. Model owners in turn wish to keep their proprietary model weights and inference code within their own secure infrastructure to protect their IP. We present a way forward for "double-blind evals", which provide cryptographic guarantees that an evaluator's prompts are not shared with the model owner, while simultaneously maintaining the confidentiality of the model weights and inference code. To accomplish this, we use secure enclaves that encrypt data in RAM at the hardware level. In a world-first pilot, we test this approach by evaluating a proprietary Google DeepMind model (Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite) against a selection of the private AILuminate benchmark corpus, using an NVIDIA H100 secure enclave on Google Cloud Platform, and using OpenMined's PySyft to maintain data and model privacy. We believe this effort marks the first use of this technology to provide mutual secrecy for one organization's frontier-class proprietary model weights and another organization's closed benchmark.
arxiv:2611.11156: Realizing federated learning (FL) in remote regions lacking reliable cellular infrastructure is challenging, as it requires dependable communication among participating devices. Low-power wide-area networks (LPWANs) offer an attractive communication solution for such scenarios. However, their limited data rates necessitate careful investigation of the communication-learning trade-offs and mechanisms to reduce communication overhead. This paper presents an investigation of the Long Range (LoRa) LPWAN technology for FL-based structural health monitoring (SHM), a representative remote IoT application. We consider a SCAFFOLD-based FL framework for multi-class anomaly detection and analyze the latency-accuracy trade-off. We also examine strategies for allocating the LoRa spreading factor (SF) during model-update exchange. Numerical results show that, with appropriate SF allocation, LoRa-supported FL-SHM can achieve competitive learning accuracy. In particular, jointly accounting for link distances and clients' dataset sizes when selecting the SF provides a favorable balance between convergence performance and communication latency. These preliminary findings offer useful insights into the design of FL systems over LPWANs for remote IoT deployments.
arxiv:2611.11477: Swarm Learning improves resilience and removes the need for a single trusted coordinator by distributing model aggregation and validation across participating nodes. However, it also delegates the validation of model updates to peers whose private data may be biased, unrepresentative, or adversarial, and existing Swarm Learning protocols generally do not attest that data, leaving decentralized validation as an attack surface. We present a robust, privacy-preserving Swarm Learning framework that makes verifiable data quality the condition for admission to the learning task. A validator joins only after a zero-knowledge attestation proves, without revealing any raw sample, that a reference model ran correctly on its private data. The attested outputs also yield a label-free class profile, so the network assembles a collectively IID validator pool from individually skewed validators as accurately as an oracle with the true labels (total-variation distance to uniform 0.025, against 0.021 for the oracle and 0.21 for random selection). Admitted validators score client updates and, through a Tendermint-style Byzantine Fault Tolerant consensus, agree on a gradient mask and a quality-derived aggregation weight for each submission, replacing dataset-size weighting with a quality-aware signal. Adapting the cut-layer idea of Split Learning, a challenge-based audit lets peers re-verify that a mask was computed on the attested data without an expensive end-to-end zero-knowledge proof. Across four benchmarks under non-IID partitions the framework matches FedAvg on clean data; under a gradient-scaling attack that collapses FedAvg to random chance, it retains 94% of clean accuracy on CIFAR-100 and over 99% on FashionMNIST, where FedAvg achieves only 2.1% and 11%. The result is a private, robust, and auditable foundation for decentralized learning.
arxiv:2611.10898: Real-world deployment of federated learning (FL) requires resilience against adversarial clients and data privacy. Byzantine fault captures the worst-case behavior of adversarial clients, while differential privacy (DP) provides statistical guarantees against privacy loss. In particular, user-level DP guards a client's entire contribution and provides more realistic protection against information leakage. Despite intensive efforts, the minimax-optimal convergence bound of Byzantine-resilient FL with user-level DP remains open. We establish an information-theoretic lower bound for any Byzantine-resilient empirical risk minimization problem under user-level DP and heterogeneous clients. We propose ByzULDP, a central DP algorithm featuring a two-level momentum across the client and server. Client-side momentum mitigates stochastic gradient variance during robust aggregation. Unlike the fault-free case, naively combining non-linear Byzantine-resilient aggregation with central DP noise can be insufficient to guarantee convergence to a bounded neighborhood of a stationary point. Our key contribution is a server-side momentum that leverages a property specific to user-level DP, where privacy sensitivity depends on how client updates are constructed, to empower convergence. ByzULDP achieves the order-optimal convergence bound for strongly-convex objectives, with vanishing error terms decaying at the optimal $O(1/T)$ and $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ rates for strongly-convex and non-convex objectives, respectively. We corroborate our analysis with numerical experiments on real-world datasets across diverse privacy budgets.
arxiv:2611.10688: Selecting a Federated Learning (FL) framework requires understanding the resource demands of its training and evaluation workflow. This work compares Flower, NVIDIA FLARE, and FedBioMed using two-dimensional MedNIST classification with ResNet-10 in a containerized, single-host environment. Following a dated review of repository activity and documented medical applications, we evaluated nine configurations per framework, with three random seeds, for a total of 81 executions. The configurations varied federation size, communication rounds, and batch size. We monitored execution time, CPU and RAM consumption, host-level GPU utilization, server network traffic rates, and model accuracy at the end of each execution. The implementations shared nominal learning settings while retaining differences in data splitting and federated evaluation. Configuration-blocked non-parametric analysis identified differences in execution time, client and server memory, GPU utilization, and network traffic rates. NVIDIA FLARE exhibited the lowest server-memory consumption and the highest host-level GPU utilization, Flower exhibited the highest average server network traffic rate, and FedBioMed required more client memory and longer execution time. No statistically significant difference in final accuracy was detected within the evaluated short training schedules; this does not establish convergence or equivalent predictive performance. The results characterize the configured workflows under shared hardware resources. They provide a concrete case study of system behavior, with conclusions bounded by workflow asymmetries, local networking, and the lightweight MedNIST workload.
arxiv:2611.12961: Federated fine-tuning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduces communication and computational overhead by training and exchanging compact trainable LoRA factors. Clients may use different LoRA ranks to meet adapter communication budgets and accommodate different local adaptation needs. The server must process these differences during aggregation and construct adapters at each client's rank for local training. We distinguish pre-aggregation alignment, which handles factor dimensions and scaling conventions before aggregation and rank-specific LoRA adapter extraction, which constructs client-sized pairs from the aggregated global model. Two common approaches to rank-specific extraction are direct rank truncation and Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of the dense update. Direct prefix truncation keeps the leading columns of one aggregated factor and the corresponding rows of the other. It is cheap but can increase reconstruction error. The dense SVD approach first forms the product of aggregated LoRA factors. It then decomposes this matrix and retains the leading singular components to construct adapters at the target rank. This gives the optimal rank-constrained approximation in Frobenius norm but incurs significant computational overhead. To address this trade-off, we propose RBLA+ as an extension of RBLA. It uses established compact QR/core-SVD decomposition to minimize Frobenius error for the extracted LoRA update without forming the dense update. It also accounts for client and server scaling conventions during upload and broadcast. Across vision and language tasks, RBLA+ improves accuracy over RBLA in multiple heterogeneous settings. In CPU benchmarks with synthetic adapters, RBLA+ has lower extraction time than the dense partial-SVD baseline. RBLA+ preserves each client's prescribed adapter size and per-round communication payload.
10.48550/arxiv.2611.10718: Anomaly detection plays a critical role in securing the Internet of things (IoT). Although existing federated principal component analysis (PCA) methods can learn the subspace of normal samples without sharing raw data, they often suffer from feature redundancy that may degrade detection performance. To address this limitation, we propose a novel and effective federated sparse Grassmann Newton (FedSGN) learning method for IoT anomaly detection. Technically, our FedSGN leverages the $\ell_{2,0}$-norm constraint on the global projection matrix to eliminate redundancy and introduces an orthogonality penalty to preserve the intrinsic structure. Moreover, we develop an augmented Lagrangian solver integrated with a semismooth Newton scheme to enable parallel client updates and Grassmann projection for robustness. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves favorable overall detection performance while reducing communication overhead. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/xianchaoxiu/FedSGN
arxiv:2611.10248: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a popular parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) method for fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs), especially in federated learning, due to its strong performance and communication efficiency. In practice, LoRA is applied to the query and value projections of transformer layers without considering the distinct roles of these components. In this work, we analyze the impact of these projections in federated fine-tuning of LLMs using LoRA and observe that the value projection converges significantly faster than the query projection. Motivated by this finding, we propose FedLoVA, a federated fine-tuning framework that trains LoRA adapters on both query and value projections locally while sharing only the value projection with the server. This approach reduces communication overhead while improving convergence efficiency. Experiments on natural language understanding, multilingual sentiment analysis, and generation tasks show that FedLoVA reduces the communication cost by up to $7.8\times$ compared to existing federated LLM fine-tuning baselines while achieving comparable or better performance. The code is available at: https://github.com/EnsiehKhazaei/FedLoVA.
arxiv:2611.09652: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has been increasingly adopted to fine-tune pretrained models with low computational cost and is therefore also preferred in the federated learning paradigm to reduce computational and communication overhead. In this work, we investigate the sparsely explored problem of the risk of private data leakage in LoRA-adapted Vision Transformers (ViTs), where low-rank updates weaken the gradient signal available to a server with access to individual client updates. We show that quality of reconstruction is limited by two coupled ambiguities: reduced information in LoRA gradients and missing spatial cues from frozen positional embeddings. To address this, we propose a spatially anchored generative inversion framework that incorporates server-prescribed trainable positional embeddings into ViT blocks during fine-tuning at clients. The resulting positional gradients act as layer-wise spatial anchors, providing additional positional cues, while the generative prior keeps reconstructions on a realistic image manifold, reducing duplicate-data and patch-permutation artifacts, {which produce similar gradients as those produced when the target client images are used}. Adding our proposed spatial anchoring to GIAS improves PSNR by 10.14 dB, SSIM by 0.45, and LPIPS by 0.098 on CIFAR-10, as well as PSNR gains of 7.83 and 11.74 dB on high-resolution CelebA and CARS datasets, respectively, in the FedSGD setting. Such gains in reconstructed image quality metrics are also maintained at higher batch sizes and in FedAvg settings. These results indicate that LoRA-based PEFT does not, by itself, prevent data leakage in FL, and carefully incorporated positional embeddings can help in exposing private information.
arxiv:2611.09552: The Information/Communication Technology (ICT) industry is severely challenging the global environment due to the sharply rising carbon emissions generated by machine learning (ML) workloads. Federated Learning (FL) is one of the prominent distributed ML systems used in applications with billions of client devices, such as Google Gboard and Apple Siri. Nearly half of the total carbon footprint in FL originates from client-side computation during local training. However, existing client selection strategies in FL primarily focus on minimizing energy consumption rather than carbon emissions, despite the fact that carbon impact depends not only on computational load but also on the underlying carbon intensity of the energy source. In this paper, we address this gap by proposing a carbon-aware fair client selection strategy (CA-FCS) designed to minimize the carbon emissions associated with model training on client devices. In contrast to existing approaches for reducing carbon emissions in FL, we incorporate hourly carbon intensity and a realistic energy consumption model developed using empirical measurements from Google Pixel smartphones to estimate client-side carbon emissions in FL. Since repeatedly selecting low-carbon clients may reduce data diversity and degrade global model performance, particularly under non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data settings, CA-FCS incorporates fairness into client selection to mitigate this issue. We conduct extensive experiments under realistic FL settings for mobile devices, where client participation is constrained by device availability conditions, such as charging status and Wi-Fi connectivity. The results demonstrate that our method reduces client-side carbon emissions by up to 46% while maintaining competitive model accuracy.
arxiv:2611.09470: Smartphones, smart-home hubs, and wearables are increasingly exposed to sophisticated Android malware, while centralized threat-detection pipelines raise privacy and scalability concerns. Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without collecting raw client data, but partial participation and variation in local model quality can destabilize global optimization. In this article, we propose DW-FedADMM, a federated optimization framework that combines primal-dual coordination with performance-dependent client-side weighting. The dynamic coefficient modulates each participating client's local state before the augmented-Lagrangian update, while the dual variables regulate disagreement between local and global model states. We evaluate DW-FedADMM on three Android malware benchmarks, namely Drebin, Malgenome, and TUANDROMD, with 5, 10, and 15 clients holding IID data shards, partial client participation, and communication budgets of 5 and 10 rounds. Each configuration is repeated with ten random seeds. DW-FedADMM obtains the highest seed-averaged accuracy on Drebin (97.64% +/- 0.20%) and the best mean accuracy in 9 of the 18 dataset-client-round configurations, including 7 of the 9 configurations with a 10-round budget. Pooled over all configurations, it reaches 95.42% accuracy, 94.62% F1-score, 96.06% precision, and 99.45% AUC, compared with 95.32%, 94.51%, 95.56%, and 99.41% for FedADMM, while also giving the lowest mean false-positive rate and the smallest client update norm among the six compared methods. Both primal-dual methods are well ahead of the averaging- and proximal-based baselines on Malgenome and TUANDROMD, where the latter often remain at the majority-class solution when clients are fragmented. The gain of dynamic weighting over FedADMM is most pronounced on Drebin and with the longer communication budget, where it also reduces the variation across seeds.
arxiv:2611.09278: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed clients without sharing raw data, making it attractive for privacy-sensitive and bandwidth-constrained applications. A practical challenge in deploying FL is reducing communication overhead while maintaining model performance under heterogeneous, non-IID data distributions. Selecting which subset of clients participates in each training round offers a principled way to address both challenges simultaneously, yet its impact on data diversity and representativeness remains underexplored. In this paper, we investigate three client selection strategies, Power-of-Choice, Fisher information, and Centered Kernel Alignment, evaluating them not only by accuracy and convergence, but through the lens of participation diversity using the Gini coefficient and KL divergence. Under non-IID conditions, restricting participation to 15% of clients per round achieves significant communication savings, and when selection promotes diverse and balanced contributions, it also improves generalization over biased alternatives. This work provides a systematic and reproducible analysis demonstrating that diversity-focused client selection renders communication efficiency and model quality complementary rather than competing objectives.
arxiv:2611.09277: Digital forensic investigations increasingly cross borders, and law enforcement agencies need to build analytical models together without centralizing their data. Federated Learning (FL) keeps data local, yet neither FL nor its frameworks enforce the jurisdictional, governance, and accountability rules that multi-agency forensic work requires. This paper takes a design-first approach to that gap. First, we derive seven requirements that a federated learning system must meet in a forensic setting. Second, we propose Federated Forensics, a three-layer reference architecture whose middle layer, unlike in existing hierarchical FL designs, sits at a jurisdictional border and can use a model update locally while blocking it from crossing that border. Third, we build a prototype of the architecture and test it on a malware-family classification task. In a prototype evaluation, the policy gate blocked every restricted update at the border with zero violations, and restricted-class accuracy rose from 0% under today's compliant alternative to 93.0%, only 4.4 points below ignoring the restriction.
arxiv:2611.08818: Federated speech emotion recognition (SER) is challenged by speaker-dependent, class-imbalanced data and by heterogeneous client devices. This paper proposes \textit{Fuzzy-FedAvg}, a server-aware framework in which the server learns Client Selection Weights (CSWs) through fuzzy Q-learning from global-model feedback. The same CSWs weight client accuracy, training time, and \divkpi{} in both client selection and aggregation, while a dedicated PCAS node manages stragglers through staleness-discounted deferred updates. On IEMOCAP and CREMA-D, \textit{Fuzzy-FedAvg} achieves higher unweighted average recall (UAR) than FedAvg in all configurations under severe non-IID conditions, and in 22 of 24 participation-level and 10 of 12 training-horizon configurations overall. It also outperforms FedProx and Oort, while SCAFFOLD and Power-of-Choice remain competitive, and it reduces cumulative training time by 81.2\% in a FedScale-based evaluation. The benefit is greatest under strong statistical heterogeneity and narrows as data become more balanced.
10.48550/arxiv.2611.10212: In recent years, singular-spectrum-based optimizers have attracted increasing attention due to their ability to preserve the matrix structure of neural network gradients, thereby enabling geometry-aware optimization. However, most singular-spectrum-based (SSB) approaches remain centralized, limiting their use in distributed learning infrastructures that exploit massive parallelism. Distributed SSB optimization is still at an early stage, with open questions about convergence guarantees and communication efficiency. To fill this gap, we propose the Distributed Momentum-based Spectral Estimator (DisMUSE), an efficient distributed SSB optimization framework for both data-center and federated settings. Using Muon-style exact orthogonalized momentum as the spectral update, DisMUSE integrates a recursive variance-reduced momentum estimator and achieves an $O((KT)^{-1/3})$ convergence rate, where $K$ and $T$ denote the number of nodes and local iterations per node, respectively. This rate matches the best-known rates for variance-reduced nonconvex distributed optimization. Building on this variance-reduced framework, we study two extensions. First, our DisMUSE method with finite Newton-Schulz (NS) iterations preserves the same convergence order under a uniform normalized support-spectrum condition, up to a multiplicative factor. Second, we develop a communication-efficient variant based on low-rank (LR) momentum transmission and quantify the error it introduces to the stationarity bound, characterizing the trade-off between accuracy and communication cost.
arxiv:2611.08783: This paper considers uplink communication design for training multiple independent machine learning models via wireless federated learning. To reduce communication delay, we utilize multi-antenna beamforming and propose a multi-model over-the-air (M-OTA) uplink transmission and aggregation method for simultaneous training of multiple models. Devices are formed into groups for local model training based on the model assignments per communication round and simultaneously perform OTA aggregation over a multi-access channel. Based on the M-OTA transmission and reception process, we formulate a joint optimization of transmit and receive beamforming and device grouping over $T$ communication rounds to maximize the training convergence rates of all models. We analyze the per-model optimality gap, which captures the impact of noisy aggregation and inter-model interference on the learning performance. We further show that the $T$-round joint optimization problem can be decomposed into per-round online optimization to devise solutions. Following this, we propose a device grouping strategy that explores channel correlation among devices to maximize OTA aggregation performance. Furthermore, we present a low-complexity iterative algorithm for joint transmit-receive beamforming with closed-form updates. Simulation shows that our proposed M-OTA approach substantially outperforms the conventional single-model sequential OTA approach and other commonly used beamforming schemes.
arxiv:2611.08771: Generative models of brain MRI are useful to understand brain conditions, and to enrich scarce and imbalanced neuroimaging data. However, training these models requires large, multi-site training sets, which is challenging. Federated learning (FL) allows for training deep learning models without sharing data. We show that training a 3D conditional latent model federatedly (where data is kept private at each site) performs similarly to centralized training (where all the data have been copied to a single site). We evaluate three metrics: conditional fidelity (how well generated MRIs perform in classification), diversity (how the generated images match the real data distribution, using MultiScale-SSIM), and realism (how close generated images are to real images, using Fréchet Inception Distance). Our results show that federated training is a viable route to develop multi-site generative models of brain MRI.
arxiv:2611.08686: Multiplayer Federated Learning (MpFL), introduced by Yoon et al. (2025), extends classical federated learning to settings where clients are rational players in a game with individual objectives and strategies, seeking an equilibrium. A natural baseline is Per-Player Local SGD (PEARL-SGD), where each player performs several local SGD steps before exchanging strategies through a central server. However, the original PEARL-SGD formulation does not extend cleanly to compressed communication. Directly compressing the players' strategies can prevent convergence to the equilibrium, even with deterministic gradients. To address this issue, we reformulate PEARL-SGD so that players communicate local strategy increments rather than the strategies themselves. Without compression, the two formulations are equivalent, but with compression, increment sharing preserves exact convergence, allowing us to design the communication-efficient compressed PEARL-SGD (C-PEARL-SGD). Beyond compression, we also consider variance reduction as another axis of improvement, introducing PEARL-SVRG and its compressed variant C-PEARL-SVRG. Under the original MpFL assumptions, we establish convergence guarantees for all variants through a unified parametric inequality. Numerical experiments, including distributed spectrum sensing, demonstrate the practical benefits of our methods over vanilla PEARL-SGD.
arxiv:2611.08383: Federated learning servers combine client models with a fixed aggregation rule, and each rule in common use is designed for one kind of heterogeneity. We study whether a large language model (LLM) that inspects the client models can choose the rule itself, without any training on the server. In FedReason, the LLM is called every ten rounds. It analyses the weights by running code in a restricted server-side sandbox, sees only the printed results, may score a few candidates on a 500-image proxy set, and submits a short Python aggregation program. The server applies the program until the next call and falls back to FedAvg whenever its output is invalid. Full weight tensors never leave the server. We evaluated FedReason with Claude Opus 5.5 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18 under Dirichlet label skew, width-heterogeneous sub-models and Byzantine clients, in 168 runs against 14 baselines. Across 12 paired label-skew runs it beat FedAvg by 1.26 percentage points on average (10 wins), and a control that spends the same per-round proxy budget on choosing among standard rules by 1.08 points. It was the strongest server-side rule on CIFAR-100 but did not beat SCAFFOLD, which changes client training. With three of ten clients malicious, it excluded all sign-flipping clients from the first round and stayed about one point below FLTrust without training a root model. Without proxy feedback, accuracy fell from 73.8% to 38.8% in one seed. A 60-round run cost 0.79 USD in API fees on average.
arxiv:2611.08021: In healthcare, protecting patient privacy is crucial due to the sensitivity of medical data and its extensive accessibility. Federated Learning (FL) offers a decentralized and privacy-preserving training paradigm, making it an ideal solution for healthcare applications. A critical challenge in healthcare is that real-world medical data often exhibits long-tailed distributions in local and global views. Existing methods addressing long-tailed FL problem typically assume that the model will be evaluated on uniform test data distribution. However, practical test data in healthcare systems is often agnostic and unpredictable, leading to potential model failures in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we introduce a novel task termed Test-Agnostic Long-Tailed Federated Learning and propose GTAFL, a comprehensive framework to address this challenge. During the training stage, GTAFL employs adaptive re-sampling, expert classifier retraining, and self-supervised learning to correct biased classifiers and distorted feature spaces caused by long-tailed training distributions. During the inference stage, an ensemble mechanism combines retrained expert classifiers to handle test data with unknown distributions. Extensive experiments on CIFAR10 and two medical datasets manifest that our framework outperforms other state-of-the-art methods. The code is available at https://github.com/cgy-lavine/GTAFL
10.1145/3843201.3856196: Integrating decentralized intelligence into peer-to-peer (P2P) energy trading requires resilient, sustainable and accountable infrastructures for Electric Vehicle (EV) networks. Existing Blockchain-Federated Learning (FL) frameworks are constrained by on-chain data bottlenecks and computationally intensive cryptographic verifications. We propose FLEET, a 3-tier hierarchical framework decoupling edge AI from the blockchain and autonomously orchestrating energy trading, local model validation, and global intelligence distribution through smart contract governance and IPFS storage. Its key feature is Proof-of-Edge-Validation (PoEV), where Charging Stations execute FL while connected EVs act as auditors during charging, resolving the trade-off between energy-efficient networking and edge AI with lightweight validation. Combined with a reputation-weighted Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) overlay, FLEET reduces on-chain cost by up to 97.9% compared to cryptographic verification baselines and sustains 2,173 TPS as the network scales up to 102 stations, ensuring sustainable networking and accountable smart contract governance.
10.64643/jatir.141288: Hazardous gases-carbon monoxide, hydrogen sulphide, ammonia, nitrogen oxides, methane, and volatile organic compounds-pose severe risks to health, industrial safety, and environmental quality, making continuous monitoring and early prediction a critical engineering priority.Conventional sensing systems, based on metal-oxidesemiconductor (MOS), electrochemical, and infrared transducers, suffer from crosssensitivity, baseline drift, and non-linear response, limiting the reliability of threshold-based alarms.Over the past decade, machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) have emerged as powerful tools for extracting selective, drift-resilient, and temporally predictive information from sensor signals, enabling accurate gas identification and multi-step-ahead concentration forecasting.This review surveys thirty recent studies (2020-2026) coupling hazardous gas sensing hardware with ML pipelines across domains including IoT-based indoor and rural air quality monitoring, underground coal mine safety, electronic nose (eNose) gas mixture identification, power transformer dissolved gas analysis, industrial emission control, and cyber-physical anomaly detection.Methodologies include classical algorithms (SVM, Random Forests, k-NN), ensembles (XGBoost, Gradient Boosting, Stacking), neural networks, and sequence-to-sequence models (LSTM, GRU, BiLSTM, BiGRU, Transformer, Autoformer).The comparison proves that hybrid and bidirectional architectures deliver better performance in multi-step forecasting tasks compared to a single model, while tree-based ensembles continue to be relevant for low-latency edge computation tasks.The review highlights the difficulties connected with sensor drifting, dataset limitations, cross-sensitivity, and the challenge of transferring models from simulated environment to the real world, suggesting future research directions in federated learning, benchmarks, explainable AI, and edge-AI compression.
arxiv:2611.07598: Federated fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) under heterogeneous client capacities is increasingly important, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) with heterogeneous ranks makes it practical. Existing server-side aggregators compose local matrix updates $ΔW_i$ from client-specific LoRA factors $(A_i,B_i)$ before aggregating them. Although these matrix updates lie in the same weight space $\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and can be averaged directly, the LoRA factors that generate them may expressed client-specific local basis. In the typical compose--aggregate--factorize--dispatch loop, this basis inconsistency can make the rank-$r_i$ reference prefix dispatched to lower-rank clients unstable after server-side refactorization. In this work, we propose \textbf{FedAbA}, a basis-consistent federated LoRA aggregation framework for heterogeneous ranks. FedAbA first extracts each client's local basis, aligns it to the corresponding prefix of the global reference basis, and constructs a basis-consistent reconstruction of each local matrix update before aggregation. It then aggregates these reconstructions with weights that combine client data size and consistency score, followed by exact coefficient-space SVD refactorization and gauge fixing before rank-prefix dispatch. Our theoretical analysis clarifies the role of basis consistency and supports the proposed consistency-aware aggregation mechanism. Extensive experiments show that FedAbA outperforms representative federated LoRA baselines, with the largest gains under the strongest rank heterogeneity.
