10.48550/arxiv.2611.07273: Quantile regression is widely used in high-stakes applications where the data are distributed across many sites and the individual records cannot be shared. The existing distributed methods for quantile regression typically require homogeneous sites, large sites, or synchronous communication, which are rarely all satisfied in practice. In this paper, we propose a new method named cloudqr. Each site summarizes its observations by a few Gaussian clouds, each given by the size, center, and covariance of a group of observations, such that the clouds match the score of the raw data exactly. A central server then fits the quantile regression on the clouds from all sites. We establish the convergence of cloudqr under mild conditions. With simulation studies and two real-world applications, we demonstrate the superior performance of cloudqr over the existing distributed methods.
arxiv:2611.10020: Secure aggregation in domains such as federated learning, Internet of Things, and voting requires operating on private inputs while preserving confidentiality, verifying that each input satisfies constraints, and avoiding trusted parties. Existing protocols achieve at most two of these requirements. We present zk-DEAP, a protocol combining lifted ElGamal homomorphic encryption, FROST threshold cryptography, and zero-knowledge proofs (Bulletproofs, zk-SNARKs, or zk-STARKs) for fully decentralized, verifiable, privacy-preserving aggregation. Our core technical contribution is a cryptographic binding mechanism preventing substitution attacks, where a valid proof for one input is paired with a ciphertext encrypting a different, malicious value. For Bulletproofs, we bind via ciphertext-derived randomness modification. For zk-SNARKs/zk-STARKs, to bind across algebraic structures (a well-known challenge in practical cryptography), we introduce a novel blinded arithmetic hash commitment with an embedded Schnorr constraint. These binding techniques force the ZKP's private witness to equal the encrypted value, ensuring any circuit-verified constraint applies to the ciphertext. We implement three production-ready, defense-in-depth variants in Rust and evaluate across 5-500 participants. Compared to unverified aggregation, zk-DEAP adds modest overhead while providing cryptographic guarantees against input manipulation that statistical defenses cannot match.
arxiv:2611.07093: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly recognized for their remarkable capabilities; federated learning (FL) offers a promising framework for collaboratively fine-tuning LLMs on edge devices while achieving data privacy. However, edge devices are inherently heterogeneous: clients may exhibit diverse data distributions and resource constraints, including limited memory and computation budgets. Recent federated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approaches address these challenges by using sparse expert activation or partial expert loading. However, existing partial-expert methods rely on heuristic full-pool observations or prioritize system-wide load balance, without guarantees for recovering client-specific relevant experts from partial observations. We propose $S^3$-MoE, a server-side sparse expert assignment framework that estimates client-specific expert relevance from partial observations and refines assignments through an exploit--explore mechanism. We also establish relevance-estimation error and exact Top-$K$ recovery guarantees. Experiments using a CNN-based MoE on CIFAR-100 show that $S^3$-MoE recovers task-dependent client--expert preferences and reduces conflicts caused by correlated expert selection across clients. Compared with Full-20 FedAvg, which gives each client access to all 20 experts for local Top-5 routing, $S^3$-MoE achieves 1.31 percentage points higher mean final accuracy while loading only $5$ experts per client.
arxiv:2611.06783: One-shot and few-round federated learning (FL) reduce communication burden by constructing a global model within one or a few communication rounds, but often achieve lower performance than conventional multi-round FL. Without frequent synchronization, client models may drift apart, causing neurons that learn similar features to occupy different positions across clients. At the same time, local data heterogeneity can cause corresponding parameters to differ in their importance to each client's predictions. Together, these challenges cause direct averaging to combine mismatched neurons and assign equal weight to parameters despite differences in their importance. We propose FedFiOT, a Fisher-weighted optimal transport framework for one-shot and few-round FL that leverages Fisher information to quantify parameter importance and guide neuron alignment and model aggregation. FedFiOT jointly optimizes neuron correspondences and global model parameters through alternating minimization of a shared Fisher-weighted objective. Theoretically, we show that FedFiOT's optimization procedure monotonically decreases the layer-wise merging objective and establish a stationarity bound that quantifies the effects of client heterogeneity and nonuniform Fisher weighting.Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over competing baselines in both one-shot and few-round federated learning settings.
arxiv:2611.06251: This paper introduces transversal passivity, a local dissipation property for regulating input and output signals to prescribed manifolds. Its supply rate is built from the transverse port errors induced by nearest-point projections, so that motion along the manifolds is not penalized. We give a necessary condition and a constructive sufficient condition for the property and relate it to existing passivity notions. For feedback interconnections through negative-adjoint linear channels, power conservation no longer cancels the transverse supply. The residual is governed by compatibility defects that depend only on the channels and the prescribed manifolds, so it can be assessed before any closed-loop analysis, and it falls into a hierarchy of exact compatibility, quadratic cancellation, and nonzero quadratic residuals. Since transversal storages are only positive semidefinite, port convergence is obtained by combining compact confinement, for instance by conserved quantities, with a dissipation margin, and we identify a geometric obstruction under which no quadratic margin is available near the feasible states. A federated learning case study with heterogeneous data shows that port convergence can be certified even though no server target is compatible with the interconnection, and that the obstruction arises for a natural choice of target.
arxiv:2611.06064: Time series forecasting is shifting from locally trained, per-series models to global models trained across many heterogeneous series, which requires learning what sets the series apart. When the raw data cannot be centralized, such a global model is trained with federated learning (FL), one client per data owner. State-of-the-art forecasters such as the Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) tell series apart through a static input that describes each series and does not change over time. In the special case of a federated setting where each client holds a single series, this static input is constant within each client and varies only across clients. We ask whether a federated TFT can learn from it. Per-batch FedAdam, which aggregates gradients after every batch, uses the static input almost as well as central training, whereas communication-efficient schemes with local epochs (FedAvg, FedAdam+Prox) extract far less from it and gain nothing significant on either application dataset. At the same local computation, an Adam-compatible SCAFFOLD keeps the static pathway responsive on wind power and gains significantly there. On building energy its error still drops, but the static pathway falls silent, so drift and communication frequency cannot be fully separated as the cause. Only per-batch FedAdam matches or beats the per-client local models across all datasets. We confirm the effect on building-energy meter data, a wind-power dataset, and a controlled synthetic dataset. The loss is not specific to the TFT: on the synthetic and the wind data two further architectures with different static-conditioning mechanisms show it as well.
10.48550/arxiv.2611.06221: Deep learning can classify crop diseases accurately from benchmark leaf images, but centralized training requires farms to share raw data, and predictions without explanations offer limited support for treatment decisions. We present FedXCrop, a federated crop disease classification pipeline that quantitatively evaluates explanations of the aggregated global model. A MobileNetV2 model trained centrally on PlantVillage achieved 99.38% test accuracy (standard deviation 0.05 over three seeds) on a fixed test set of 5,428 images across 38 classes. Federated models initialized with ImageNet weights were trained for 30 rounds across five clients. FedAvg achieved 98.81% accuracy with identically distributed clients and 98.81%, 98.59%, and 97.78% under Dirichlet label skew (alpha = 1, 0.5, and 0.1, respectively). FedProx was not significantly different from FedAvg at any heterogeneity level (McNemar p > 0.3). Grad-CAM and SmoothGrad explanations were evaluated on 380 test images. Both attributed more energy to the leaf than chance (0.70-0.78 versus 0.60), while Grad-CAM maps from federated and centralized models showed Spearman correlations of 0.74-0.76. Agreement decreased as heterogeneity increased, lesion localization was only modestly above chance, and a model-randomization test indicated that SmoothGrad maps depended substantially on image structure rather than learned parameters. In this setting, label skew reduced federated accuracy by 0.6-1.6 percentage points relative to centralized training. FedAvg largely preserved Grad-CAM behavior, while FedProx provided no measurable benefit.
arxiv:2611.06169: Domain-specific adaptation of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in privacy-sensitive edge environments requires federated fine-tuning, yet client selection remains challenging due to heterogeneous multimodal data and modality availability, dynamic system conditions, and evolving client utility during training. We propose Constraint-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Efficient Federated Fine-Tuning (CARE-FL), a constrained online client-selection framework for federated MLLM Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning. CARE-FL formulates client participation as a sequential decision process and employs Q-value decomposition to address the large combinatorial joint action space through scalable client-level long-term utility estimation. These utilities are learned online using a modified Double Deep Q-Learning (DDQL) scheme, while constraint-aware $ε$-greedy execution selects feasible client subsets under per-round latency and bandwidth constraints. Complementing client selection, an adaptive aggregation mechanism further controls potentially unstable global updates and places greater weight on the previous model when needed. Experiments on the CrisisMMD disaster-response task in emulated heterogeneous wireless edge environments show that CARE-FL achieves higher and more stable test accuracy than the compared client-selection baselines across different system settings, while satisfying the imposed latency and bandwidth constraints.
10.48550/arxiv.2611.05841: This vision paper argues that distributed learning, including federated and decentralized, should become a first-class paradigm in LLM post-training, not merely a privacy add-on. Current methods like RLHF and DPO rest on an invisible assumption: preference data should be centralized. We contend this assumption is scientifically unjustified, practically unsustainable, and ethically problematic. As LLMs deploy into healthcare, law, finance, and multilingual communities, preference data originates from populations that cannot or will not centralize. We develop a three-pillar argument grounded in (1) privacy and data sovereignty, (2) pluralism and representational equity, and (3) robustness and scalability. We formalize key technical challenges unique to this intersection, reference drift, preference heterogeneity, and the DP-utility trade-off for contrastive losses, and propose concrete algorithmic directions, and sketch a research agenda. Our analysis shows distributed post-training is not only necessary but tractable, and ignoring it risks AI that is legally noncompliant, representationally narrow, and brittle at scale.
arxiv:2611.05546: Decentralized federated learning (DFL) eliminates the central aggregation server but remains vulnerable to data heterogeneity, Byzantine attacks, and channel noise. We show that noise accumulates as models propagate across nodes, becoming increasingly significant as the learning rate decays. Moreover, accumulated noise enables Byzantine attackers to exploit loss-based model selection by mimicking honest model averages. To address these challenges, we propose screened, hop-aware, ranked, proximal averaging, a robust DFL framework (FedSharp). In this approach, each node maintains models from its 2b predecessors, ensuring at least b honest candidates when at most b nodes are Byzantine. FedSharp screens suspicious models using coordinate-wise median deviations, averages the b lowest-loss candidates to reduce fresh channel-noise variance by a factor of b, and applies noise-adaptive gradient-norm regularization and proximal training to mitigate accumulated noise and non-IID drift. Experiments on a 100-node ring with 33 Byzantine nodes show that FedSharp achieves 93.5-94.9% accuracy on MNIST, compared with 29.4-38.1% for a state-of-the-art single-model-selection benchmark, and 32.8-48.8% on CIFAR-10, compared with 10.0-30.5%, across Gaussian and hidden attacks under IID and non-IID data. On MNIST, FedSharp also achieves accuracy within approximately one percentage point of the benchmark operating without channel noise.
arxiv:2611.05544: In this paper, three operations on Gibbs probability measures are studied: renormalization, normalized log-linear combination, and nesting. The resulting measures are shown to be Gibbs probability measures with explicit expressions for their objective functions, reference measures, and regularization factors. These measures are further characterized as unique solutions to optimization problems involving linear combinations of the original objective functions, subject to either relative entropy regularization or relative entropy constraints. When the reference measures are probability measures, geometric interpretations of these three operations are established involving Pythagorean identities and exponential geodesics.A central result is the equivalence between nesting and normalized log-linear combinations of Gibbs probability measures. These results are then applied to supervised machine learning with Gibbs algorithms, which are represented by Gibbs probability measures. In this context, either through nesting or log-linear combinations, Gibbs algorithms trained on local datasets are used to form new Gibbs algorithms trained upon the aggregation of all local training datasets. Interestingly, the parameters of such operations, determine the weights of each training data point on the aggregated dataset. %Operations on local Gibbs probability measures are shown to control the contributions of training data. This observation is leveraged for achieving: (a) exact machine unlearning in centralized, decentralized, and federated learning systems; and (b) centralized-equivalent performance, in the sense of producing algorithms trained on the aggregation of all local datasets in decentralized and federated learning .
arxiv:2611.05035: Deep learning in medical imaging is constrained by data scarcity and by privacy regulations that make centralizing patient data across institutions impractical. Federated Learning (FL) addresses these constraints by keeping data local, but its distributed nature exposes training to strong statistical heterogeneity. Multicentric medical data is particularly affected, exhibiting a mixed skew that combines feature, label, concept, and quantity shifts across centers. Personalized FL mitigates heterogeneity by tailoring a model to each client, yet most methods assume training from scratch, which is unrealistic given the high dimensionality of medical features relative to the limited data available. We propose the Personalized Aligner Federated Pretrained (PAFP) framework, a personalized FL approach built on a pre-trained backbone. PAFP inserts client-specific Feature Alignment modules before the fine-tuned blocks to realign hidden feature distributions toward a server-aggregated target. On the FedISIC benchmark, PAFP attains the highest unweighted balanced accuracy while reducing inter-client performance variance roughly six-fold relative to the strongest baseline, yielding accuracy and cross-client equity jointly. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Alexandre-Leclercq/PAFP.
arxiv:2611.04667: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative training of machine learning models across distributed clients while preserving data privacy. In practical deployments, FL relies on selecting a client subset in each communication round to reduce communication cost, mitigate stragglers, and improve training efficiency under heterogeneous data and system conditions. In heterogeneous edge computing environments, both statistical heterogeneity and system heterogeneity significantly affect convergence efficiency and model performance. However, existing client selection methods often address these factors independently, overlooking their coupled and dynamic impact across communication rounds. To address this limitation, we propose FedCSGA, a Client Selection method for Federated learning based on Genetic Algorithm. FedCSGA encodes client subsets as chromosomes and evaluates these subsets through a non-linear fitness function that jointly integrates resource-aware metrics and history-aware participation weighting. This design captures subset-level interactions, mitigates persistent selection bias, and balances statistical utility with system efficiency. Extensive experiments on FMNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet demonstrate that FedCSGA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse heterogeneity settings, achieving accuracy improvements of up to 7.0% and faster convergence with fewer communication rounds. These results validate the effectiveness of jointly modeling statistical and system factors to achieve robust and efficient learning in heterogeneous federated environments.
arxiv:2611.04285: Histogram estimation is a fundamental primitive in distributed data analysis, with applications in counting queries and federated learning. In many settings, the universe of categories is enormous, yet each user's data involves only a small subset, yielding sparse local histograms. This raises a natural question: To what extent can local sparsity reduce the communication needed to estimate the global histogram? We answer this question by characterizing the communication complexity of distributed sparse histogram estimation under prescribed $\ell_1$ distortion and failure probability constraints. Our upper bound is achieved by a randomized covering scheme that optimizes how accurately each user represents its local histogram to reduce communication. By exploiting the distortion budget directly rather than imposing unbiasedness, the scheme achieves lower communication costs than standard unbiased sampling and hashing constructions. We establish the scheme's first-order optimality through a lower bound based on local support identification. The key step is to relate communication cost directly to the number of active coordinates revealed by each user's message, rather than to bound information about the aggregate via distance-based Fano's inequalities. This characterization further quantifies how the communication advantage of heterogeneous over homogeneous encoders varies across parameter regimes.
arxiv:2611.04448: We consider deterministic composite federated optimization, in which distributed smooth client objectives are combined with a shared, possibly nonsmooth, regularizer. We propose Relative-Error Composite FedDyn (REC-FedDyn), an inexact method that supports partial participation, with one server-side proximal evaluation per communication round. REC-FedDyn employs a directly testable relative-error criterion that allows each client to independently control the accuracy of its local subproblem, without a server-side acceptance test. We establish almost-sure iterate convergence for strongly convex and convex problems, almost-sure asymptotic stationarity for nonconvex problems, and communication and parallel gradient-evaluation complexity bounds, all under partial participation and without assuming bounded data heterogeneity. Experiments on image inpainting, fMRI prediction, and neural-network classification with structured regularization demonstrate efficiency and robustness across levels of data heterogeneity and client participation.
10.48550/arxiv.2611.09992: Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) improves radio access network flexibility through disaggregation, open interfaces, and programmable RAN Intelligent Controllers (RICs). However, the same openness and distribution increase the attack surface and make centralized intrusion detection difficult to scale across heterogeneous RAN sites. This paper presents a federated lightweight Transformer framework for privacy-preserving network-layer cyberattack detection in O-RAN. Each participating site trains a compact Transformer locally on temporally ordered network-flow records, while only model parameters are shared with a federated coordinator. To model realistic site heterogeneity, the client datasets are partitioned according to a Dirichlet distribution, resulting in non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) local data. The local detector uses feature projection, positional encoding, multi-head self-attention, feed-forward layers, and temporal pooling to classify five network-layer attack categories: ICMP, Slowloris, SYN, TCP-ACK, and UDP. Experiments on the NetsLab 5G O-RAN intrusion-detection dataset show an overall accuracy of 94.89 % and a macro-F1 score of 81.09 %.
arxiv:2611.03586: Federated learning (FL) runtimes standardize aggregation and deployment, but each new study still requires federation formation: selecting task-eligible sites and preparing their local data and task code for federated training or analysis. This preparation recurs when the target changes, while raw records and site-private mappings are excluded from cross-site FL messages. We present FedReady, a system that performs federation formation with bounded LLM agents. Agents propose shared contracts, local adapters, and task code; the runtime owns workflow state and accepts artifacts only after checks tied to their digests. Candidate site discovery prioritizes recall; local eligibility verification checks task support before site admission. Once participating sites and artifacts are fixed, conventional federated training or analysis proceeds without readiness agents. Across 39 simulated retinal sites and four tasks, discovery reaches recall 1.00 at precision 0.65; local eligibility verification removes all 17 false positives without losing an eligible site-task pair. The participating sites supply 45,575 task-record instances and complete four 100-round jobs, including one with a runtime-generated contract. Across ten patient cohorts, preparation supports seven patient populations and holds endpoints at three sources as unsupported. Comparison with manually prepared reference populations and analysis (the manual reference) gives a maximum survival-curve difference of 0.001133. We also analyze 19 development failures, targeted classification ablations, and standalone and heterogeneous agent configurations. These results establish the feasibility of task-specific data preparation before ordinary FL training or analysis.
arxiv:2611.03273: Federated learning (FL) is well suited to Internet of Things (IoT) sensing. However, devices carry different sensors and come online in periodic patterns, and as such, the sensors among the participants change from round to round. Under naive averaging, devices without a sensor overwrite its parameters, and a single-sensor device never learns how its sensor relates to the others. Existing methods either redesign local training for mismatched sensors (assuming always-available devices) or select clients without regard to their sensors. We propose Tier-aware Intra-pod Decoupled Encoders (TIDE). Specifically, each sensor has its own encoder and auxiliary head, whose parameters are merged only within the "pod" (i.e., the devices that hold the sensor), while the fusion layer and the task head remain shared by all devices. On three multimodal activity recognition datasets against eight baselines, TIDE reaches 78.06% on ActionSense, 7.63 points above the next method, is the most accurate on all three datasets at half its own communication, and at equal communication leads on ActionSense and is ahead within seed variation on the other two.
arxiv:2611.03024: Over-the-Air Federated Learning (OTA-FL) improves communication efficiency by exploiting waveform superposition over wireless Multiple-Access Channels (MAC). However, client heterogeneity, fading, energy constraints, and participation imbalance can degrade both fairness and aggregation accuracy. Existing Pareto-oriented fair OTA-FL schemes may still suffer from large aggregation distortion when highly weighted clients experience poor channel conditions. This paper proposes DisC, a game-theoretic distributed client selection framework for fairness-aware, channel-aware, and energy-efficient OTA-FL. Each client selects its participation level by maximizing a utility that captures Pareto fairness importance, learning relevance, OTA distortion, energy consumption, and delay. We show that DisC admits a Nash equilibrium and can be formulated as an exact potential game, where stable equilibria correspond to locally optimal OTA-FL operating points. DisC therefore offers a distributed, incentive-compatible alternative to centralized client selection under wireless and resource constraints.
arxiv:2611.03015: Most fuel oil consumption (FOC) models for voyage planning are per-ship models and thus generalize poorly beyond each vessel's records. Transfer and federated learning have been reported to perform better, but under different protocols that often use inputs unavailable before departure or random data splits. It therefore remains unclear which approach performs best. In this study, we compare 11 per-ship, adaptation-based, and global methods on 21 vessels. To prevent leakage, all methods receive identical inputs known or forecast before departure, excluding engine RPM and shaft power, and are tested on intact voyage legs after all training records of each vessel. Global pooling, in which one model describes each vessel by its ship identity and seven ship specifications, performs best overall in every setting examined. For in-fleet vessels, Global LightGBM reaches an overall MAPE of 8.92%, against 11.14% for Per-Ship LightGBM, and outperforms every per-ship and adaptation-based model. Global models of five architectures, including a Transformer, all outperform the per-ship and federated models. Fine-tuning a global model for each vessel, even by low-rank adaptation of the Transformer, adds no accuracy. Without any records of a vessel, the global model reaches a median MAPE of 11.20% and outperforms a per-ship model trained on that vessel's records for 14 of 21 vessels. Adding its first records to the pooled data is as accurate as vessel-specific adaptation. Ship identity and specifications are largely interchangeable for in-fleet vessels, but only the specifications support zero-shot prediction. Its error grows as a vessel's specifications differ from the fleet's. Per-ship models and vessel-specific adaptation are therefore unnecessary under fair comparison. One global model can serve a whole fleet, including newly delivered vessels with similar specifications.
arxiv:2611.02790: Robust driver-state modelling requires synchronized physiological, behavioural, and contextual signals, yet existing open resources typically target a single cognitive state, omit continuous vehicle context, or do not define evaluation protocols that expose inter-subject heterogeneity. We present Multimental-IAS, a multimodal driver mental-state dataset collected in a cockpit-in-the-loop simulation built on CARLA. It contains vehicle telemetry with scenario-context channels, four-channel EEG and three-channel PPG from a Muse 2 headband, and cabin-facing video from 23 participants, recorded in 148 trials (11.6 hours) under six induced states: Normal, Distracted, Alerted, Stressed, Relaxed, and Drowsy. We document the acquisition pipeline in detail and provide a benchmark with one protocol for all models: chronological within-subject splits, participant-disjoint cross-subject folds, validation-based model selection, and ablations over modalities, scenario-context channels, and signal normalization. Multimodal fusion reaches a macro-F1 of 0.94 for drivers seen during training. For unseen drivers, fusing driving dynamics with per-window normalized EEG/PPG raises macro-F1 from 0.408 (telemetry alone) to 0.485, consistently across all five folds, while the gap between the two protocols quantifies the inter-driver heterogeneity that personalized models must address. Multimental-IAS thus provides a concrete testbed for non-IID generalization, personalization, and federated learning in driver monitoring.
arxiv:2611.02412: Federated Learning (FL) offers a paradigm for collaborative machine learning model training among clients, preserving data privacy by avoiding direct data sharing. However, the gradient information exchanged in FL has been shown to be vulnerable to Gradient Inversion Attacks (GIA), which can reconstruct sensitive user data. To counter these threats, various privacy-enhancing technologies like Secure Multi-party Computing (SMC), Homomorphic Encryption (HE), and Differential Privacy (DP) have been integrated into FL. While effective, these methods often introduce significant trade-offs between privacy and model utility. By revisiting the key to privacy exposure in FL under GIA, which lies in the frequent sharing of model gradients that contain private data, we take a new perspective by designing a novel privacy-preserving FL framework that effectively ``breaks the direct connection'' between the shared parameters and the local private data to defend against GIA. Our proposed framework, HyperFL++, leverages hypernetworks to generate local model parameters, where only the hypernetwork parameters are aggregated by the server. To ensure practicality, HyperFL++ incorporates a Row-wise Kronecker Decomposition (RKD) to mitigate the memory and communication overhead from the hypernetwork. Comprehensive theoretical analysis and extensive experiments validate our method's effectiveness in protecting data privacy while maintaining high model utility. Our code is available at https://github.com/Pengxin-Guo/HyperFL/tree/hyperfl%2B%2B.
10.48550/arxiv.2611.03032: Multimodal fusion is studied under hybrid federation, where data are partitioned across samples and feature blocks. The proposed two-dimensional federated smooth multiple-kernel large-margin learning method (2D-FedSMKL) integrates availability-corrected modality scores, group-kernel regularization, and smooth worst-site risk aggregation. For fixed maps and propensities, the objective is convex and smooth. Curvature bounds and exact synchronous block-gradient equivalence are established for binary and multiclass scores, giving a conditional accelerated rate. An oracle-propensity binary risk bound and a propensity-perturbation result are also derived. Simulations and two public activity-recognition benchmarks assess site heterogeneity and modality absence. Worst-site aggregation improves worst-site performance under heterogeneity, including reversed and size-balanced designs. On the benchmarks, validation selects the correction; the selected model is not significantly worse than the strongest reference at the worst site, and group-regularization benefits vary by dataset.
10.48550/arxiv.2611.02598: We study the classical Local Stochastic Extragradient method (Local SEG) for monotone variational inequalities under intermittent communication, where devices perform several local oracle calls between synchronization rounds. For affine monotone mean operators, including nonsymmetric bilinear saddle systems, we prove that equal device averaging commutes pathwise with both stages of the stochastic extragradient update. Local trajectories may therefore drift apart while their mean follows a centralized stochastic-extragradient recursion driven by averaged noise. The identity remains valid when individual oracle realizations are nonlinear and query dependent. Under conditionally centered oracle errors that are conditionally independent across devices within each stage, the reduction yields a restricted weak-gap rate that uses the local sequential depth for deterministic progress and the aggregate oracle budget across devices for variance reduction. When every device makes at least two local oracle calls per communication round, the bound contains no additional mixed client-drift term and is also attained by a terminal-only aggregation schedule. An affine Gaussian lower bound matches the depth and sample dependences before statistical saturation for distributed zero-respecting algorithms; its statistical component applies to arbitrary randomized algorithms. A complementary lower bound for feasible distributed zero-respecting methods shows that bounded geometry and query-dependent noise can create an additional communication-locality obstruction. These results delineate the exact-averaging regime of unconstrained affine Local SEG and a complexity boundary that arises under active feasibility constraints.
arxiv:2611.02146: Personalized federated learning (PFL) may improve client-level performance, but deeper personalization increases deployment cost. We formulate personalization-depth selection as a utility-based empirical decision problem in which client utility equals Macro-F1 minus a cost-sensitivity weight times deployment cost, over six personalization depths labeled P0 through P5. We compare fixed policies with an offline per-client Oracle reference and report allocation maps over Dirichlet data heterogeneity and cost sensitivity. Although evaluated on this hierarchy, the formulation can accommodate any finite candidate set. On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and a PTB-XL subset, personalization shows empirical, setting-dependent decision regimes rather than a universal benefit: higher cost sensitivity shifts Oracle mass toward the global-only depth P0; low cost sensitivity can favor deeper actions. Patterns are grid observations (three seeds per cell), not theoretical boundaries. Best-uniform is competitive with Oracle assignment (6.5 percent plus or minus 7.8 percent relative regret; 95 percent confidence interval 5.9 to 7.1), whereas random and personalize-all incur much larger regret (189.3 percent plus or minus 367.1 percent and 409.0 percent plus or minus 803.2 percent). Under the same utility, Ditto full-model personalization is substantially suboptimal once cost is counted. The contribution is an offline characterization of when personalization depth is worth its cost, not a new PFL optimizer or deployment-time scheduler.
arxiv:2611.01893: Domain skew challenges federated learning by requiring a shared model to accommodate distinct visual distributions. Domain-specific experts can capture these distributions separately, creating an opportunity to integrate their representations in a unified predictor. We propose Federated Knowledge-Preserving Learning (FKPL), a two-stage framework that combines domain-oriented expert training with prototype-based classifier calibration. First, a one-shot subspace-based clustering procedure groups clients for intra-cluster training. The resulting expert encoders are concatenated and frozen, preserving each learned feature mapping during global integration. Second, clients interpolate their concatenated features with class-matched domain prototypes and upload the resulting virtual features. The server trains a global linear classifier on these features, concentrating classifier optimization at the server after a single feature upload. FKPL achieves average accuracies of 73.01\%, 67.00\%, and 64.51\% on Office-Caltech-10, PACS, and a four-domain subset of DomainNet, respectively. On DomainNet, its cross-domain standard deviation is 7.50 percentage points, the lowest among the evaluated methods. With the same concatenated extractor, prototype-based calibration improves average accuracy over federated classifier training by 9.99 and 14.94 percentage points on Office-Caltech-10 and PACS. These results identify classifier calibration as an effective way to combine preserved domain representations into a global predictor.
arxiv:2611.01853: This paper presents a privacy-preserving mood monitoring framework that classifies emotional states from ECG-derived heart rate variability (HRV) features. The framework is evaluated on three public datasets comprising 74 participants and further validated using a wearable device in a pilot study. Leave-One-Participant-Out cross-validation (LOPO-CV) is used to assess generalization to unseen individuals. A series of experiments investigates the impact of temporal windowing, HRV feature selection, and class balancing on both four-class valence-arousal and binary valence classification. Results show that class balancing substantially improves minority-class recall, while Logistic Regression consistently outperforms five alternative classifiers and achieves competitive performance against HRV-based baselines. Pilot validation using a Polar H10 wearable achieves 75% binary valence accuracy on an unseen individual without calibration, demonstrating the feasibility of real-world deployment. To preserve privacy, the framework is also implemented using federated learning on a six-node Raspberry Pi cluster. Federated Logistic Regression achieves performance comparable to centralized training without sharing raw physiological data. These results demonstrate the potential of interpretable and privacy-preserving mood monitoring for continuous mental health assessment in clinical and community settings.
arxiv:2611.01812: Hierarchical federated learning (HFL) enables communication-efficient training in unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms, but performance degrades under changing and heterogeneous environments. This paper proposes domain-aware HFL (DA-HFL), integrating mobility-informed clustering, cluster-level aggregation, cloud-based Fisher-weighted merging, a domain-adversarial shared backbone, environment-specific heads, and gated inference with local adaptation. A mission-weighted optimization formulation incorporates energy, latency, and cluster-head eligibility constraints. Theoretical analysis establishes resource feasibility, a conditional backbone-stationarity bound, the quadratic optimality of Fisher-weighted merging, and communication and computation complexity bounds. Simulations across four heterogeneous environments demonstrate faster convergence, improved accuracy during environmental transitions, and more stable, purer clusters than the evaluated baselines, with modest energy overhead over resource-aware HFL. Ablation studies validate the contributions of the proposed components.
arxiv:2611.01082: Anonymous credentials can hide which registered client participates in federated learning, but their unlinkability also makes repeated misconduct difficult to associate. We present VeilFL, a two-aggregator protocol that adds staged accountability to PINE (USENIX Security '24). Each submission binds two private PINE messages, a round-specific pseudonym, and a tracing pair to the same hidden credential secret. This design enables detection of duplicate submissions within a round without introducing a persistent identifier for normal participation. VeilFL implements accountability in two stages. After a confirmed duplicate or joint PINE rejection, a threshold tracing committee reveals a stable handle that links faults associated with the same credential. The client's registered identity is recoverable only after the public log records the requisite number of linked faults and a separate threshold committee authorizes identification. Accepted and unopened submissions remain unlinkable under the stated assumptions. This work establishes submission binding and duplicate detection, anonymity, fault non-frameability, controlled two-stage opening, and preservation of PINE's privacy and validity guarantees. In the prototype implementation, creating a submission requires a median of 2.11 ms, while verification requires 3.01 ms. Batch verification reduces the cost to 1.86 ms per submission for a batch of 1,000. The public part of each submission is 608 bytes, with 1,248 bytes of additional VeilFL protocol data across the two aggregator submissions. Each opening stage completes within 4.3 ms for the different committee configurations.
arxiv:2611.01040: In the emerging 6G paradigm, where AI-driven services operate over decentralized and resource-constrained infrastructures, the convergence of distributed learning algorithms remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces $\mathrm{ParaBlock}$++, a low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite-assisted hierarchical federated learning (HFL) framework, enabling resource-limited terrestrial clients to collaboratively engage in federated learning (FL) via ground-satellite links (GSLs) supported by LEO satellite megaconstellations. Within this architecture, LEO satellites serve multiple roles: as edge servers aggregating and broadcasting models, as clients accelerating training, and as high-throughput relays managing inter-satellite routing through inter-satellite links (ISLs). Departing from conventional synchronous Jacobian-type updates, $\mathrm{ParaBlock}$++ employs asynchronous BCD-type updates to enhance convergence speed. We provide theoretical convergence guarantees for convex, strongly convex, and non-convex objectives, and formulate optimization problems to determine optimal cluster resource allocation and model partitioning for minimizing global training latency. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that $\mathrm{ParaBlock}$++ achieves faster initial convergence and comparable final performance for deep neural networks (DNNs) such as ResNet-18, offering promising directions for federated learning across geographically remote areas enabled by 6G technologies, but much less global rounds and communication cost.
arxiv:2611.01025: With the emerging 6G paradigm where AI services operate over decentralized and resource-constrained edge infrastructure, performance of distributed learning algorithms remains a significant challenge. This paper proposes HAFL, a Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite-assisted hierarchical asynchronous Federated Learning (FL) framework, enabling resource-limited terrestrial clients to collaborate via Ground-Satellite Links (GSLs). Within this framework, LEO satellites serve multiple roles: as edge servers aggregating and broadcasting models, as clients accelerating training, and as high-throughput relays managing inter-satellite routing through Inter-Satellite Links (ISLs). Unlike conventional synchronous Jacobian-type updates, HAFL employs asynchronous Gauss-Seidel-type updates to enhance convergence speed. We provide theoretical convergences for convex, strongly convex, and nonconvex objectives, respectively, and formulate optimization problems to jointly determine optimal hyperparameters to minimize global training latency. Evaluations demonstrate that HAFL achieves faster initial convergence and comparable final performance for benchmark DNNs and datasets, offering promising FL systems across remote areas with 6G technologies, but much less global rounds and communication cost.
10.48550/arxiv.2611.00712: We study federated model-free learning of a common linear quadratic regulator (LQR) gain under a limited uplink communication budget, with clients that share dynamics and costs but experience different process-noise levels. Conventionally, clients transmit gradient matrices whose dimension equals the number of controller parameters. Exploiting the structure of two-point zeroth-order estimates, we consider an implementation in which clients transmit only one scalar cost-difference coefficient per rollout pair, while the server regenerates the associated perturbation directions from shared seeds. Communication thus scales with the number of rollout pairs rather than the controller dimension, turning the uplink budget into a rollout budget. Because noise heterogeneity produces gradient estimates of widely differing variance and every client carries equal weight in the fleet objective, uniform rollout allocation allows noisy clients to dominate the aggregated update and increases the probability of destabilizing updates. We propose a rollout-allocation scheme that assigns rollout pairs in proportion to the standard deviation of each client's estimates and show that it minimizes the variance of the aggregated update. The scheme is implemented exactly through a greedy integer allocation rule whose weights are estimated from the communicated scalars. We further prove that a single allocation factor quantifies its improvement over uniform allocation in a one-round instability bound, the certified step size, and the error floor of a joint stability and convergence guarantee. Simulations show that, under the same communication budget, personalized allocation reduces the one-step instability rate from $37\%$ to $0.3\%$.
arxiv:2610.41570: Decentralized federated learning (DFL) has emerged as a scalable alternative to centralized federated learning, removing the single point of failure and communication bottleneck at the server. However, most existing decentralized approaches rely on full-neighborhood broadcasting, where each client transmits its model update to all of its neighbors in each communication round. While effective, this results in significant communication overhead and high energy consumption. This paper applies spectral graph tools as lightweight client selection methods that leverage the graph topology by analyzing the spectral properties of the graph Laplacian over a fixed communication graph. Specifically, we exploit eigenvector embeddings and heat/diffusion kernel similarities to guide each client in selecting only a subset of structurally relevant neighbors, i.e., those that are most beneficial for the convergence of the federation process. This topology aware randomization matches or outperforms uniform neighborhood subsampling and approaches the accuracy of full broadcasting. The largest gains, about $3$ percentage points, emerge under strong data heterogeneity on larger, structurally rich graphs, while the total number of transmitted messages is reduced by $50\%$ compared to naive broadcasting.
arxiv:2610.41278: Federated learning (FL) keeps raw data local, but most deployments still rely on a trusted coordinator for client admission, checkpoint distribution, update collection, aggregation, and rewards. This paper presents AuditFL, a contract-backed clearing layer for auditable FL in open settings. AuditFL keeps training and aggregation off chain, stores model artifacts in an assumed reliable off-chain artifact store, and records only content identifiers and economic state on chain. Clients reserve update tickets with deposits, publish update identifiers, and later claim refunds or rewards; the task coordinator publishes global checkpoints and finalizes rounds through deterministic settlement rules. The design does not remove the aggregator, but makes its on-chain round decisions attributable, replayable, auditable, and economically constrained. We implement AuditFL as both a deterministic state-machine prototype and a Solidity contract on a local Ethereum-compatible Anvil chain. On full MNIST with Dirichlet non-IID splits, 12 rounds, and up to 200 clients, AuditFL preserves the Plain FL learning trajectory while its overhead follows closed-form control-plane models. At 200 clients, the contract run issues 5,026 transactions, stores 2,413 off-chain artifacts (144.9 MiB), and consumes 829.7M EVM gas, dominated by per-client reserve and publish calls. Controlled dropout, invalid-update, and artifact-unavailability stress tests reduce inclusion nearly linearly but still finalize rounds, with final-accuracy changes remaining within a few tenths of an accuracy percentage point even under high injected failure rates.
arxiv:2610.41193: Multimodal federated learning (MFL) trains a shared model by aggregating client updates without exchanging raw data. Under missing modalities, clients adapt active modality encoders and a shared prediction block (fusion and classifier) to different input subsets. This raises two server-side questions: which clients should contribute to each component, and how should their aggregates be incorporated across rounds? We observe that an absent-modality encoder can still adapt through missing-input handling. Availability- based aggregation can therefore omit its update while retaining jointly learned prediction-block updates. Contributor selection also shapes server momentum, a weighted history of aggregated updates. We observe that prediction-block momentum can improve or reduce performance depending on the encoder update policy. We therefore propose Role-Aware Server Optimization (RASO), which coordinates contributor selection with role-specific server updates. RASO selects contributors through prediction dependence and inclusion in local optimization, retains encoder momentum, and synchronizes the shared prediction block to its current aggregate. Experiments across datasets and fusion architectures demonstrate the effectiveness of RASO under missing modalities.
10.66414/mls.978-1-0666009-1-5_4: The growth and integration of cloud computing with other advanced technologies (such as Artificial Intelligence (AI) and other security technologies and architectures) have introduced different cybersecurity challenges and opportunities that require academic investigation. This research conducts a bibliometric analysis of 1,583 papers from Scopus database between 2010 to 2026 trying to address four main research aims: (1) publication growth and productivity, (2) active contributors in the field, (3) themes and evolution of cloud security, and (4) emerging and research directions. The findings reveal an exponential growth, with annual output rising from 3 papers in 2010 to 358 in 2025, highlighting an annual growth rate exceeding 30%. Keyword analysis also reveals technical security evolutions: from cloud architecture and basic security (2010–2015), through threat, privacy, risk and intelligent detection (2016–2020), to current state dominated AI-driven approaches and other cutting edge technologies such as blockchain, edge computing, quantum cryptography and decentralized security (2021–2026). The results also show increased security complexity due to the integration of advanced technologies and secure architectures with the cloud such as decentralized security (e.g. federated learning also known as distributed AI models), AI driven cybersecurity, zero-trust architectures, privacy-preserving computation and advanced cryptography such as post-quantum cryptography. These technologies are among the most challenging emerging research areas, yet they are the most promising regarding cloud computing. Finally, as cybersecurity technologies evolve, security complexity of the cloud will continue to grow.
arxiv:2610.41039: As Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models are increasingly deployed in distributed environments, from federated learning to edge-cloud systems, their architecture harbors an underexplored landscape of security vulnerabilities. Moving beyond textual analysis, we uncover structural memorization: a novel vulnerability where a fine-tuned model memorizes not only its training data but also the internal pathway used to process it, creating a characteristic routing fingerprint unique to the training process. We provide comprehensive empirical evidence that structural memorization emerges consistently even from a few samples, and that its intensity is directly influenced by the choice of trainable modules. We show that these memorized expert pathways can be stealthily recovered through the model's unconditional generation, using only routing and output logits, with no knowledge of the fine-tuning data or procedure. In distributed deployments, this vulnerability is amplified as routing information is exposed at multiple trust boundaries, including federated aggregation points, edge-cloud interfaces, and multi-tenant monitoring systems. Recovery exposes a critical blind spot: traditional membership inference metrics, viewed through the lens of expert routing, fail to identify memorized data corresponding to these structural pathways. To close this gap, we devise composite metrics combining reference model tail likelihood with complexity-aware normalization, significantly improving detection of memorized routing structures. This enables adversaries to pinpoint critical experts shaped by fine-tuning, whether dominant or dormant, and execute targeted attacks such as router manipulation or backdoor injection in realistic distributed settings where attackers lack training data but can observe routing patterns across system components.
arxiv:2610.39985: Federated learning traditionally relies on a fixed aggregation rule despite shifting client state and wireless dynamics. We present FedMaJ, a framework that dynamically selects aggregation rules via Majority Judgment voting. During voting rounds, clients evaluate candidate models across performance, resource utilization, channel condition, and fairness metrics. The server adopts the majority-preferred rule and retains it until the next vote, scheduled dynamically based on accuracy trends. Evaluated in over-the-air federated learning with explicit energy and resource cost modeling, synthetic and Fashion-MNIST experiments show that FedMaJ achieves competitive learning performance and superior aggregation-influence fairness. Under extreme-evaluation perturbations, Majority Judgment yields significantly more stable rule selections than mean-based scoring, establishing ordinal voting as a robust control layer for adaptive aggregation.
arxiv:2610.39791: Predicting human mobility is central to network management, urban planning, and location-based services, yet privacy concerns are increasingly pushing such tasks toward federated learning. A key challenge in this setting is the strong heterogeneity of mobility data across users, which leads to non-IID data distributions and can significantly impact model performance and fairness. In this paper, we present a large-scale measurement study of device-level mobility heterogeneity using data from a major MNO in a dense European capital. Our dataset comprises mobility traces derived from network events, covering over 50,000 UEs across 178 smartphone models. We group devices into tiers based on their market segment and show that mobility characteristics, such as spatial range and regularity, vary systematically across these tiers, revealing a previously underexplored source of bias in mobility data. We investigate the implications of this heterogeneity on the use case of federated next-location prediction. In particular, we find that balancing device tiers across silos through tier-aware client selection yields the best results, improving fairness by up to 34.49% without degrading accuracy. In contrast, a FedProx-only approach achieves a 21.46% fairness improvement, offering a reasonable alternative when device information is unavailable, though with lower overall gains.
arxiv:2610.39483: Automated detection has become the essential safeguard against realistic synthetic media, but deploying it at scale requires training on sensitive data from multiple organizations, putting privacy and the transparency demanded by forensic review in direct conflict. Federated learning resolves the privacy side by sharing only model updates rather than raw data, but whether this comes at the cost of trustworthy gradient-based explanations, which analysts rely on to decide whether or not to trust a flagged clip, has not been studied. We present the systematic study of Grad-CAM explanation faithfulness under federated deepfake detection, evaluating an EfficientNet-B4 detector on FaceForensics++ across five federated clients under varying degrees of data heterogeneity. We find that the relationship between federation and explanation quality is non-monotonic: at near-IID (Independent and Identically Distributed Data) and moderate heterogeneity, federated models match or exceed the faithfulness of a centralized baseline, but at extreme heterogeneity, explanations break down entirely, becoming spatially incoherent and, on average, causally misleading. This degradation is not a general cost of federated training but a threshold effect tied to client heterogeneity, and we offer practical guidance for identifying when privacy-preserving deepfake detection can be deployed safely and when its explanations can no longer be trusted. Code and data partitions are available for reproducibility.
10.1117/12.3133751: Aiming at the problems of scattered speech, limited privacy and strong noise interference in college English listening, a distributed listening recognition model based on federated learning is constructed. The system adopts a Conformer acoustic coding and CTC-Attention hybrid decoding structure, and achieves end-to-end recognition through spectral enhancement and robust feature modeling. To deal with Non-IID data, an improved FedAvg aggregation algorithm is designed, and the distribution consistency constraint and joint loss function are introduced to improve the global convergence stability. At the same time, gradient quantization and sparsity are adopted to reduce communication overhead, and differential privacy is combined to achieve secure parameter interaction. The experimental results show that this framework significantly optimizes the convergence speed and word error rate under multi-terminal conditions, verifying its engineering effectiveness.
10.1117/12.3134525: This study discusses the difficulties of energy effectiveness, device Variability, and privacy of data in distributed demand forecasting systems for the Industrial Internet of Things enabled by 5G(IIoT). Federated Education (FL)-based collaborative framework is proposed, enhanced with Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) to optimize client selection, task scheduling, and energy consumption in highly dynamic oilfield environments. The framework uses multi-agent DRL to balance energy efficiency and prediction accuracy, so as to realize real-time decision-making and adaptive orchestration of IIoT devices. Gradient compression techniques are used to minimize communication overhead without affecting model performance. Experimental validation on a synthetic oil production dataset shows that the proposed framework reduces energy consumption by 60% while maintaining prediction accuracy, with a tradeoff rate of only 5% compared to traditional FL methods. The framework improves the convergence speed, and the number of training cycles is reduced by more than 50% compared with baseline models such as FedAvg and FedProx. These findings confirm the effectiveness of DRLdriven optimization in meeting the special needs of Internet of Things (IIoT)-based oilfield operations. This study provides a reliable and scalable method to predict collaborative demand in distributed Internet of Things (IIoT) systems. The potential of the framework in improving operational efficiency and data privacy is significantly demonstrated due to the integration of multi-agent DRL and energy-aware orchestration mechanism, allowing intelligent decision-making in complex oilfield environments.
10.1117/12.3133741: Federated learning, explainable artificial intelligence, and reinforcement learning are increasingly shaping the landscape of neurosurgical brain-computer interface (BCI) applications. To address the major issue of personality rights protection, this study proposes a data-based, privacy-preserving BCI neurosurgical risk analysis and clinical governance framework. A federated learning protocol is provided for secure aggregation and analysis of multi-center EEG and fMRI data while maintaining the data sovereignty of the institutions. The system uses SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to provide transparent explanations of risk factors. The impact of high-frequency neural oscillations and functional connectivity patterns on the vulnerability of personality rights is the focus. The reinforcement learning module dynamically optimizes the clinical decision path to achieve actionable governance. Experimental results from a multi-institutional dataset show that the technology achieved 92.3% accuracy in risk prediction and reduced ethical conflicts by 38.7% in simulated clinical workflows. The combined framework not only improves the technical performance of risk assessment, but also improves the application compliance of intelligent neural technology in ethical supervision and regulation. This research lays the foundation for the use of reliable, interpretable and adaptive AI systems in the sensitive environment of BCI neurosurgery.
10.1117/12.3135688: Aiming at the common engineering challenges of data silos, privacy leakage, untraceable authorization and insufficient model interpretability existing in social credit assessment scenarios, this paper constructs a distributed secure credit evaluation system integrating block chain and federated learning. A federated aggregation algorithm based on homomorphic encryption is proposed to support privacy-preserving collaborative modeling across multi-institution platforms. Meanwhile, a smart contract-enabled authorization mechanism is established to realize full lifecycle data traceability and standardized service compliance. Verified on the UCI German Credit Dataset, the proposed system achieves an AUC value of 0.83, which is 9.2% higher than that of traditional centralized architectures. In the scenario of 5000 concurrent credit assessment requests, the system throughput reaches 2800 TPS with an end-to-end delay of 350 ms. Superior to conventional schemes in assessment accuracy, operational performance and data security, the system can provide a reliable technical reference for practical social credit assessment applications.
10.1117/12.3134727: This paper investigates advanced privacy protection and data security mechanisms for artificial intelligence-based psychological counseling systems. The study designed a hierarchical security framework that integrates technologies such as hybrid encryption, dynamic multi-dimensional anonymization, adaptive access control, differential privacy federated learning, and automated compliance auditing to address the technical challenges of the entire data lifecycle. The proposed techniques are experimentally validated on large-scale anonymized datasets in a secure cloud infrastructure to simulate distributed and centralized application scenarios. The experimental results show that the method has little impact on the model accuracy and computational performance, and at the same time, it has a significant reduction in the risk of adversarial inference rate and data leakage. The combination of federated optimization and strong cryptographic protocols effectively reduces centralized data vulnerabilities and enhances distributed privacy protection. The automated audit mechanism ensures traceability and compliance of the system in all running stages. These findings suggest that it is essential to protect sensitive mental health data driven by artificial intelligence. These findings set a benchmark for the secure engineering of digital mental health services.
arxiv:2610.39902: Clients observing different parts of a prediction task may learn locally equivalent models with incompatible behavior outside their observed support. We study whether redundant models permit local low-loss paths toward a compatible shared model. CovFedAvg retains local models and curve controls on clients, fits a common endpoint through aggregated gradient contributions, and selects an actual candidate model using distributed training losses. No centralized calibration examples or client-to-client sample exchange are required. Exact selection guarantees no higher evaluated training loss than the previous model and the current-round FedAvg candidate; this is not a global-optimality, stationarity, generalization, or differential-privacy guarantee. We state conditional client-compatibility and approximate-selection bounds and retain corrected transformation identities and a separate full-gradient safeguard theorem for reference algorithms. A complementary input-support example recovers the shared absolute-value regression, while matched direct fine-tuning also solves it. Across a synthetic support task, recorded activity-recognition subjects, and participating and future gas-sensor batches, we evaluate five methods, five seeds, two network widths, and 20 rounds without calibration data. At width 16, CovFedAvg raises participating-Gas macro balanced accuracy from FedAvg's 88.88% to 89.84%; matched distributed fine-tuning reaches 91.65%. Results support feasibility and modest gains over FedAvg, but do not establish a curve-specific advantage over equally costly optimization. Exact-sum numerical experiments establish data flow; end-to-end privacy requires additional mechanisms and analysis.
arxiv:2610.39716: AdaGrad-style methods can simultaneously adapt to both the order and constants of smoothness in centralized optimization. However, existing extensions to federated optimization with heterogeneous client objectives and multiple local steps require the smoothness order to be specified in advance. We address this limitation with AdaFed, a federated method that adapts across several regimes under a single choice of parameters. In the deterministic setting, AdaFed achieves an $O(1/T)$ convergence rate for both smooth nonconvex and smooth convex objectives, and an $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ rate for Lipschitz nonsmooth convex objectives up to logarithmic factors. Under a light-tailed stochastic-gradient noise assumption, these guarantees extend to the stochastic setting with additional logarithmic factors and noise-dependent terms. Experiments across the three problem classes further support our theoretical findings.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.39680: Emerging intelligent wireless networks increasingly rely on autonomous AI agents to adapt spectrum usage to dynamic and heterogeneous operating conditions. However, collective learning is challenging when agents experience different local interference environments and cannot exchange raw observations due to communication-overhead and privacy constraints. We propose Federated Agentic Spectrum Coordination with Interference Awareness (FASCIA), a federated multi-agent deep reinforcement learning framework for adaptive spectrum coordination. In FASCIA, each network manager acts as an autonomous AI agent that perceives its local interference environment, accumulates experience in a persistent local memory, and learns an adaptive spectrum coordination policy through local interactions. Coordination among agents is achieved through periodic federated aggregation of locally trained models, without exchanging raw sensing data or experience. Since spectrum decisions made by one agent alter the environments observed by others, local learning is inherently heterogeneous and coupled. FASCIA employs proximal regularization to mitigate the resulting model drift and explicitly accounts for inter-carrier interference arising from partially overlapping channels. FASCIA is the first federated agentic AI framework to address this challenging interference-coupled spectrum coordination setting. Extensive simulations demonstrate that FASCIA achieves performance close to the centralized benchmark while avoiding raw-experience exchange and maintaining effectiveness across heterogeneous network configurations.
arxiv:2610.39008: Tabular-to-image encoding methods, which transform tabular data into image-like representations, have shown promising results in predictive tasks. Despite their benefits, these methods follow a centralized paradigm, in which the data are collected and models are trained on a central device. This raises privacy and security concerns, particularly the risk of data leakage, unauthorized data collection and access to users' private information. Federated Learning (FL) provides a decentralized framework in which multiple clients jointly optimize a shared model without directly sharing training data. We introduce Fed-IGTD, a horizontal FL-based approach in which clients share a common feature space and upload only local statistics, from which the server reconstructs the global correlation matrix and obtains a feature-to-pixel mapping to train a convolutional neural network via Federated Averaging (FedAvg). We studied two differential privacy (DP) mechanisms: (i) a one-shot Gaussian mechanism protecting the correlation-aggregation step; and (ii) a client-level DP-FedAvg variant protecting the training with privacy loss composed via a Renyi-DP accountant. We evaluated Fed-IGTD on five datasets under a systematic sweep of non-IID severity and privacy budgets. Privacy protection applied to the mapping-construction step has little impact on predictive performance. By contrast, DP-FedAvg substantially degrades utility at moderate privacy budgets with a small client cohort (K=5). Ablation study indicates that this degradation is driven mainly by the injected noise rather than by uniform averaging or update clipping. Macro-F1 exhibits sensitivity to performance degradation than accuracy under non-IID heterogeneity and class imbalance.
arxiv:2610.38970: Current and emerging mobile networks face increasing privacy, scalability, and performance challenges as distributed learning becomes essential for advanced 6G services. These challenges are amplified by the presence of non-IID data, naturally arising in heterogeneous wireless environments, that degrade the performance of standard Federated Learning (FL) approaches. To address non-IID data across clients, we propose a Clustered Federated Learning (CFL) framework that assigns clients to specialized models during training. Data-domain clustering initializes model-based clustering, enabling identification and exploitation of client similarities without sharing raw data while reducing communication cost. Motivated by mmWave beam selection, we evaluate our methods on a wireless simulation dataset (DeepMIMO) and complement it with two non-IID benchmarks (FEMNIST, Rotated CIFAR-10) to isolate different non-IID characteristics. Our best configurations improve accuracy over IFCA by 4.8 pp on DeepMIMO and 10.6 pp on FEMNIST while reducing downlink data volume by 83.1 % on FEMNIST compared to IFCA. We demonstrate that different clustering strategies suit different non-IID characteristics. These results show that our CFL methods enable resource-efficient, and high-performance distributed learning in future 6G networks.
arxiv:2610.38793: Distributed machine learning (DML), including conventional distributed training and federated learning (FL), enables collaborative model development across cloud-edge-IoT systems without fully centralizing raw data. However, distributing data, computation, updates, and orchestration increases the attack surface and introduces coupled challenges across privacy, robustness, reliability, fairness, and governance. This survey presents a security-centered, heterogeneity-aware roadmap for trustworthy DML, with FL treated as a prominent high-risk case. We first characterize the assets, adversaries, trust assumptions, and coordination patterns that define DML/FL security boundaries. We then analyze how statistical, system, and trust heterogeneity, including non-IID data, resource asymmetry, intermittent participation, and cross-silo/cross-device trust differences, affect convergence, fairness, attack detectability, and defense reliability. Next, we synthesize attack-defense interactions across poisoning, backdoors, Byzantine manipulation, privacy leakage, model extraction, network/orchestration attacks, Sybil behavior, and strategic participation. We further compare layered defenses, including robust aggregation, drift-aware optimization, differential privacy, secure aggregation, homomorphic encryption, secure multiparty computation, trusted execution environments, watermarking, provenance, authenticated communication, and monitoring. Finally, we discuss deployment, evaluation, governance, and open research guidelines, emphasizing reproducible, non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) partitions, attack-aware benchmarks, privacy budgets, attack success rate, client-level disparity, latency, communication, memory, energy/carbon overhead, and auditable lifecycle artifacts.
arxiv:2610.38686: Streaming federated learning (SFL) allows clients to train a shared model from continuously arriving data without retaining large local datasets. Such streams often exhibit temporal dependence, yet its effect on generalization remains poorly understood. In this paper we study the expected generalization gap of the aggregated model when client data follow Markov processes, using information-theoretic and rate-distortion techniques. Our framework accommodates heterogeneous Markovian dynamics across clients and distinguishes temporal dependence from information acquired during local learning. We establish bounds under cross-entropy loss, specializing them to Linear Next-Token Prediction (LNTP) and Self-Attention Next-Token Prediction (SANTP). These results quantify the effects of client count, communication rounds, sample size, data dimension, mixing time, and context length. In particular, they reveal a communication--generalization tradeoff: although frequent aggregation may help optimization, it can weaken generalization guarantees. They also suggest a potential advantage of distributed over centralized streaming learning under a fixed total data budget. Temporal dependence enters through the square root of the mixing time. By analyzing the history-state process, we obtain refined bounds with improved context-length dependence under suitable mixing conditions. Experiments on GPT-style language-model pretraining with TinyStories and real-world time-series forecasting illustrate how collaboration and communication frequency influence generalization under temporal dependence
arxiv:2610.38411: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without exchanging raw data, but conventional FL provides limited runtime governance, evidence verification, fairness assessment, explainability monitoring, and auditability. This paper proposes Governance-Aware Federated Learning (GAFL), which combines independent governance-evidence verification, temporal trust, fairness and explanation assessment, anomaly detection, policy enforcement, normalized aggregation, and tamper-evident audit logging. Client-reported governance values are authenticated, bound to their submitted model updates, and independently recomputed before aggregation. A cross-silo prototype with 10 participants was evaluated on the Adult Income dataset under honest, benign non-IID, biased-data, malicious-update, non-compliant, falsified-evidence, and mixed-threat scenarios. Four methods were compared across five random seeds: FedAvg, FedAvg with anomaly filtering, GAFL without independent verification, and complete GAFL. Complete GAFL intervened on all affected participants at the final round across the evaluated risk scenarios, including identifying 100% of falsified-evidence participants, whereas GAFL without verification identified none of the falsified-evidence participants. Final macro-F1 ranged from 0.7520 to 0.7733 across GAFL scenarios. Complete GAFL required 173.67 plus or minus 26.94 ms of governance processing per round, compared with 3.82 plus or minus 0.79 ms for FedAvg. A strict demographic-parity threshold also caused frequent interventions for honest participants, demonstrating a significant fairness-policy and utility trade-off.
arxiv:2610.38172: Federated Learning (FL) allows for secure analysis of distributed data without data sharing. We and others have successfully applied FL to neuroimaging tasks, such as Alzheimer's disease classification from structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). FL trains a deep learning model locally at each site, encrypts the local model parameters and sends them to a federation controller that aggregates the local models under homomorphic encryption, the resulting community model is sent back to the sites for further training, and the process repeats for a number of rounds. FL often achieves learning performance (e.g., accuracy) close to centralized training, but no data leaves the sites and model parameters are protected through encryption and other measures. In this paper, we show that federations composed of sites with heterogeneous amounts of data (1 large site plus small sites) perform better than homogeneous (same data per site) federations, particularly in low data regimes, while reaching performance close to centralized training. Having a big site often results in faster convergence and higher final accuracy. Heterogeneous federations better exploit sites with small amounts of data, a common situation in large consortia such as ENIGMA.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.38789: Differential privacy (DP) has become the standard for privacy-preserving data analysis, yet its practical implementation in federated or distributed settings often faces a significant utility gap compared to the central model. While existing frameworks, including local, shuffle, and secure aggregation models, offer vetted primitives, they can incur high error for important tasks such as selection. Our first contribution is to show that this is inherent in the aggregation model: any private selection algorithm relying on the standard noisy aggregation primitive requires $Ω(\sqrt{d}/\varepsilon)$ samples. To address this limitation, we propose adding a new primitive that implements a version of the Sparse Vector Technique (SVT) and argue that it has simple implementations under various trust models. We demonstrate its power by developing an $\varepsilon$-differentially private algorithm for the selection problem. For selection in dimension $d$, our algorithm achieves an additive error of $O\left(\frac{\log(dn)}{\varepsilon}\right)$, matching that of the central model when $n$ is polynomially bounded in $d$. Furthermore, we show that this can be done using a near-optimal expected number $O(d\log^*d)$ of SVT queries.
