Across prototype monitoring, signal-security analysis, and simulated collaboration, the programme shows that privacy layers can be composed without collapsing diagnostic utility, while exposing overhead and fidelity limits that constrain clinical translation.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.25318: Attacks using ransomware have developed into complex multiphase campaigns that target vital infrastructure, resulting in annual damages of billions of dollars. Conventional detection techniques are ineffective against zero-day variations, and privacy issues are raised by centralized machine learning algorithms. Federated learning allows for cooperative model training without data sharing, however current FL approaches suffer from explainability issues, high communication cost, and non-IID data heterogeneity. In this study, we present AdaFedXplain, an explainable AI-based adaptive federated learning system for ransomware detection. Our approach includes progressive XGBoost complexity to avoid overfitting, a decaying learning rate schedule for stable convergence, and dynamic client grading based on ransomware prevalence and data sufficiency. Using 62,485 real-world ransomware samples from four OS-based non-IID clients, we compare AdaFedXplain against FedAvg, FedProx, and SCAFFOLD. According to experimental data, AdaFedXplain outperforms all baselines with 99.59% detection accuracy and 99.64% F1-score while cutting energy usage by 75%, latency by 65%, and communication overhead by 75%. The ablation investigation demonstrates that every element enhances performance. Security analysts can use SHAP explainability to identify important PE header characteristics that influence detection decisions. Our system provides a collaborative ransomware detection solution that is efficient and interpretable, while reducing privacy risks through federated learnings data-local training paradigm.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.26953: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training while preserving data privacy. However, non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data inevitably introduces classifier bias, leading to significant performance degradation. Existing studies primarily focus on calibrating or reconstructing the classifier after FL training to alleviate this bias. We find that the last-layer representations of the global model are often suboptimal for establishing a global decision boundary. Instead, classifiers constructed based on intermediate-layer representations can achieve superior performance. This finding provides a critical insight into overcoming the performance bottleneck inherent in existing paradigms. Nevertheless, identifying the optimal layer without auxiliary datasets or prior knowledge remains a formidable challenge. In this paper, we propose FLARE (Federated Cross-Layer Joint ClAssifier REconstruction) which rethinks classifier reconstruction from a cross-layer perspective and generalizes ridge regression to jointly exploit cross-layer representations, thereby surpassing the performance of any individual layer. Specifically, after FL training, clients perform only a single forward pass to extract class-conditional statistics from predefined layers. The server aggregates these statistics to construct a joint cross-layer ridge classifier, where an adaptive coupling coefficient regulates cross-layer correlations, thereby facilitating the integration of complementary discriminative information. Extensive experiments across 11 datasets, 8 model architectures, and diverse data heterogeneity scenarios demonstrate that FLARE, as a plug-and-play post-processing method, improves accuracy by 11.35% with only one additional communication round.
arxiv:2610.25264: Malware image classification (MIC), in which binary files are converted into visual representations and deep neural networks are trained to identify malware families, has recently emerged as an effective approach for malware detection. Federated learning (FL) enables malware image classifiers to be trained collaboratively by multiple clients without sharing raw data. However, a fundamental challenge in FL is data heterogeneity (non-IID), which is particularly relevant but understudied in the malware context. In this paper, we address this gap via three contributions. First, we present an empirical study of federated MIC under varying degrees of data heterogeneity across three popular malware image datasets (MalImg, Virus-MNIST, and MalNet). We show that while FL achieves strong accuracy under IID conditions, both accuracy and training stability degrade as data becomes increasingly non-IID. Second, we introduce a set of round-level statistics that characterize the data contributed by participating clients in each FL round, and demonstrate that class entropy (diversity of class labels present in a given round) exhibits strong positive correlation with global model accuracy. Third, leveraging this insight, we propose an entropy-aware client selection strategy that filters candidate client subsets based on class entropy, and show that our strategy outperforms standard random selection. Our results highlight the role of client composition in federated MIC and underscore the importance of distribution-aware classifier training under data heterogeneity.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.24841: Fine-tuning directly on user-side data is an effective way to improve the performance of widely adopted data-driven human mesh recovery (HMR) models. However, doing so for existing HMR methods often assumes aggregating user-side data from real-world HMR-deployed devices to a central training server, posing a significant privacy risk as sensitive human images are transmitted. How can human mesh recovery be evaluated and improved in privacy-constrained real-world settings? We study this question through a benchmark in which state-of-the-art HMR models are trained with federated learning and a secure-aggregation variant, neither of which centralizes raw images, and evaluated across a wide range of client-scale and data-heterogeneity settings. We document that common HMR training pipelines are built around centralized data access and quantify how representative HMR backbones behave when that assumption is removed. Furthermore, to study the data bottleneck of privacy-constrained HMR training, we propose DePoser, a local annotation and fine-tuning pipeline enhanced with depth foundation models, with which collaboratively trained HMR models can be locally tailored to the end user's distribution. On in-the-wild data, fine-tuning on DePoser annotations improves personalization accuracy, measured against DePoser-generated pseudo-ground truth. This benchmark aims to support future work on privacy-constrained HMR models and their real-world deployment and evaluation.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.24536: Federated learning has recently emerged as an important paradigm for large-scale distributed model training, which can be naturally formulated as a class of distributed learning problems. The alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) is a widely used approach for solving such problems. However, its practical performance is often hindered by significant communication overhead and system heterogeneity. In this paper, we propose a multi-step inertial ADMM algorithm, called MiFedADMM, for federated learning. The proposed method leverages multiple historical iterates on the server side to construct a higher-order extrapolation after each aggregation to accelerate the convergence behavior. Under mild assumptions, we establish convergence results for the single-step variant of the proposed method and derive an O(1/K) convergence rate. Numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and improved performance of the proposed method compared with existing approaches.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.24643: A widely repeated account of membership inference holds that models lean on fine-grained detail for samples they have memorized, so degrading an input's resolution should expose membership through how quickly a prediction falls apart. We test that account band by band. A monotone family of zero-phase low-pass filters is applied to each query image, the target's confidence on its original prediction is read at every step, and the resulting decay is scored in a dozen ways. Two federated ResNet-18 targets are studied, one trained normally and one pushed to a 45.1-point generalization gap. The account does not survive. On the normally trained target the best profile score reaches an AUC of 0.513 against 0.537 for a single confidence threshold, and on the overfit target 0.735 against 0.943. A search over 1206 candidate scores, with direction chosen on a held-out half and a fitted combination as an upper bound, produces no score that beats the threshold in either regime. The failure has a mechanism: the mean confidence gap between members and non-members grows as detail is removed, exactly as the hypothesis predicts, but the spread grows faster, so discriminability falls from the first step onward. Decomposing each image into phase and magnitude shows why no band-localized operation can work, since the advantage travels with image structure, surviving at 0.567 when the phase is kept and collapsing to 0.492 when only the magnitude is. Membership is a whole-image identity effect rather than an accumulation of spectral energy in any band, and defenses aimed at high-frequency reliance are aimed at the wrong target.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.26916: Space-based artificial intelligence (AI) is moving beyond isolated onboard processing toward constellation-scale computing over optical inter-satellite links (OISLs). Yet current infrastructures remain fragmented, making end-to-end (E2E) coordination across heterogeneous and multi-vendor systems difficult. This article examines the StarMind vision and develops a reference framework for distributed orbital computing. It organizes the system into five layers and defines six standardizable interfaces that link mission intent to resource conditions and trustworthy result delivery. The framework also clarifies the operational constraints that determine whether orbital cooperation is worthwhile. In a representative synthetic aperture radar/interferometric SAR (SAR/InSAR) case study, the framework reduces E2E latency to 41-min, compared with 61-min for localized onboard computing and 146-min for ground-based processing. This gain does not rely on faster processors in orbit. Instead, it comes from reducing contact waiting and urgent Earth downlink traffic through resource-aware task placement and gateway selection. Feasibility analysis shows that the proposed framework is more effective when source datasets are large, output products are compact, and optical inter-satellite link capacity is sufficient. When these conditions are absent, conventional processing may remain preferable. Finally, we discuss research opportunities in joint task partitioning and cross-domain orchestration, hierarchical federated intelligence, and large model-enabled intelligence to advance an interoperable space-ground computing continuum.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.22848: Wireless Digital Twins are emerging as a key enabler for predictive network control in 6G Vehicle-to-Infrastructure (V2I) systems. However, closed-loop V2I DTs face two dual-stage communication bottlenecks arising from model parameter exchange for V2I DT reconstruction and multi-service V2I traffic delivery after each reconstruction. This paper proposes a closed-loop dual-stage End-to-End (E2E) latency optimization framework that integrates Compressed Personalized Federated Learning with a unified Large-Language-Model-guided Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning approach. A CPFL-enabled decision-oriented V2I DT is first constructed by jointly predicting Path Loss (PL) and Quality-of-Experience (QoE)-oriented Key Performance Indicators (KPIs). Then the framework comprises two temporally coupled but latency-wise distinct optimization stages: Stage I minimizes the joint Uplink (UL) and Downlink (DL) E2E transmission latency of compressed shared backbone's parameters, and Stage II minimizes the service-aware E2E latency of multi-service V2I traffic. As the two stages share aligned agent roles and action space, we develop a unified Semantic-Aware Guidance-Enhanced Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization framework, in which the LLM acts as a training-time semantic planner that provides high-level traffic splitting and power allocation guidance to reduce inefficient exploration, while the MARL agents execute feasible low-level actions. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework enables efficient V2I DT reconstruction and significantly reduces both E2E latency for DT reconstruction and multi-service V2I traffic. The proposed SAGE-MAPPO supports cross-stage policy reuse by sequentially solving the two stages within each DT update cycle, which accelerates convergence relative to the existing baselines and facilitates timely DT updates in dynamic V2I scenarios.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.22906: Federated Learning (FL) is a powerful machine learning framework that allows building a global model from the contributions of multiple, distributed clients, while ensuring the privacy of their local data. However, its heavy computational and communication overheads challenge its use for contemporary AI workloads such as natural language processing (NLP) and multimodal analysis. For this reason, this paper presents a novel small language model that leverages byte-level text and multimodal data processing, enhanced by a linear attention mechanism, to enable manageable Federated Learning of NLP and multimodal analysis tasks. The proposed model, nicknamed FederatedBytes, manages to process text and any other data types, including images, by treating its input as a mere sequence of bytes, while its lean linear attention mechanism allows abating the overall memory and computational footprint. To prove the effectiveness of the proposed model we have carried out an extensive performance evaluation on sentiment analysis tasks in multilingual and multimodal settings over the Multilingual Amazon Reviews and ScienceQA datasets. The experimental results show that FederatedBytes has been able to outperform comparable models such as ByT5 and LSTM, achieving higher accuracy while significantly reducing memory and communication overheads.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.23434: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative training of complex models across large-scale networks of edge devices while keeping data localized. However, data heterogeneity and high communication overhead remain fundamental bottlenecks. Recently, the spectral optimizer Muon has demonstrated remarkable advantages over Adam-like methods in centralized training. While recent efforts have attempted to transition Muon to FL, naive integrations into traditional architectures fail short. Crucially, existing approaches do not support the the communication compression and local steps --- the two foundational techniques of efficient FL. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel spectral FL method that utilizes both local updates and compression. We establish rigorous convergence guarantees under mild assumptions, notably eliminating the restrictive bounded heterogeneity condition. Empirical evaluation on standard image classification benchmarks validates the efficiency and robustness of our approach.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.22996: Minimizing the wall-clock time required to reach a target accuracy is crucial in federated learning (FL), where many applications require frequent model updates as data distributions evolve over time. Nevertheless, in heterogeneous environments, slow clients with limited computational and communication capabilities can delay global synchronization, forcing faster clients to wait and increasing the overall training time. To mitigate this straggler effect, recent studies have introduced per-round time constraints and adapted client workloads within the available time. However, these approaches primarily focus on local computation, whereas communication can become a major bottleneck in communication-limited environments, motivating the joint optimization of training workload and communication compression. Although previous studies have explored such joint optimization, determining an effective training--communication balance under a fixed per-round time budget remains challenging, as the resulting model performance depends on both training progress and compression-induced degradation. We therefore propose TALLOP, which jointly optimizes the local training workload and communication compression under per-round time constraints. TALLOP predicts the training loss achievable under different computation budgets from the early-stage mini-batch loss trajectory (LENS), and estimates the degradation caused by communication compression using a compression-error model (CLEN). TALLOP combines these predictions to select the training-communication allocation that minimizes the post-compression loss under the given round time constraint. Experiments in heterogeneous FL environments show that TALLOP generally achieves competitive or improved time-to-accuracy compared with approaches that optimize only local training or neither, although the benefit over training-only adaptation depends on the setting.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.24036: Federated learning (FL) trains a shared model across data-owning clients without centralizing raw data, but client data difficulty and compute budgets can differ. We study local early-exit Vision Transformer (ViT) inference, where an intermediate classifier may return a prediction before the final Transformer stage. The proposed method replaces one global acceptance threshold with a client-specific base threshold from label entropy and shallow-exit confidence, then adjusts each input using predictive entropy, confidence, top-two class margin, and exit depth. Aggregation uses only clients that updated a parameter. Security-aware routing reaches 88.70% CIFAR-10 accuracy with 32.0% depth saving and 73.7% ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy with 30\% saving. On matched six-client non-IID CIFAR-100, full-depth accuracy is 72.28% versus 68.20--71.80% for four heterogeneous-FL baselines; robustness-aware routing reaches 70.01% with 32.55% saving.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.21455: In this paper, we develop an alternating minimization algorithm for federated sparse orthogonal nonnegative matrix factorization (ONMF) with emphases on controlling client drift. To reduce communication frequency, clients perform multiple local updates between communication rounds, biasing updates toward their respective local objectives and giving rise to client drift, particularly under data heterogeneity. In federated sparse ONMF, global nonsmooth regularization further complicates drift control, as proximal mappings generally do not commute with averaging. To address these challenges, we develop an effective optimization algorithm that introduces variable splitting to decouple proximal operator evaluation from communication, allowing clients to handle joint sparsity regularization locally. In addition, the algorithm incorporates a correction term into the local gradients to adjust the update directions and mitigate client drift. We theoretically establish that the proposed algorithm achieves sublinear convergence to a bounded residual error under some mild conditions. Numerical experiments demonstrate favorable convergence behavior on a synthetic dataset and competitive clustering performance on real-world multi-view datasets.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.21832: How long should each client train before communicating? Federated learning usually answers with a fixed, hand-tuned number of local epochs, yet an extra epoch helps only while the loss it removes outweighs the client drift it adds. We cast local training as finite-horizon optimal stopping: a client trains while the next epoch's expected loss reduction exceeds its priced squared drift. We prove that this one-stage look-ahead threshold is optimal whenever stopping decisions are nested, derive closed forms for geometric and power-law returns, and show that an estimated rule loses utility only through wrong-signed decisions. Epoch-level evidence supports the model's structure (geometric diminishing returns and additive drift) and reveals a simple regularity: the stage of training, not the client, sets the budget. The resulting rule, FedStop, is never more than one point below tuned FedAvg in mean accuracy. Where its budgets vary, it raises worst-decile accuracy by 4-8 points over tuned FedAvg and an adaptive-interval baseline, and every one of these gains remains significant after a Holm correction. Against the client-side stopping rules ALT and FLASH, it has the highest CIFAR-10 worst decile on every seed and is level elsewhere. It stays stable where per-client early stopping collapses, and each stopping decision takes constant time.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.21059: The twin goals of privacy-preserving federated learning (FL) -- harnessing distributed data while protecting the parties who contribute it -- demands three properties: model privacy, data privacy, and integrity. Achieving all three in a realistic deployment -- with a single coordinator and millions of users -- remains an open challenge that prior work has yet to fully resolve. We present NOMAI, the first scalable MPC-based FL system to provide all three guarantees simultaneously. NOMAI operates under an honest-majority assumption in the semi-honest model, with an extension to the malicious-with-abort setting. At its core, NOMAI combines a multi-committee MPC architecture with packed Shamir secret sharing, enabling SIMD-style secure computation that scales far beyond what monolithic n-party protocols can support. We further introduce ML-aware optimizations and new cryptographic primitives that substantially reduce per-user overhead. Our evaluation shows NOMAI is practically deployable at unprecedented scale: it reduces per-user computation to just <350 ms (semi-honest) and <700 ms (malicious) for per iteration of training MNIST, achieving three orders-of-magnitude improvements over prior work while seamlessly supporting populations of over 106 users. This demonstrates, for the first time, that MPC-based FL can meet the scale demands of real-world systems without compromising on privacy or integrity.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.21742: Echo State Networks (ESNs), as lightweight implementations of reservoir computing, provide efficient solutions for temporal data processing in resource-constrained environments. While standard ESNs offer computational efficiency, their dense readout layers inflate the stored model and the per-sample inference cost. This paper introduces a Smooth-L1 regularized ESN (SL1ESN) that promotes sparsity in the readout layer while preserving differentiability for gradient-based optimization. The method employs a twice-differentiable Smooth-L1 approximation compatible with Newton's method, which we exploit both for centralized training and for a second-order (Newton-step) federated aggregation scheme. Under a single fixed shrinkage threshold shared by every dataset and both settings, experiments on seven time-series classification benchmarks show that SL1ESN learns readouts that are 77-95% sparse in the centralized setting and 75-95% sparse in the federated one. On five of the seven benchmarks, the mean accuracy of the sparse readout over ten seeds differs from that of the stronger dense baseline by at most 0.7 points in the centralized setting and 1.6 points in the federated one, differences of the same order as the seed-to-seed variation, while on the remaining two it trails by 2.4-5.8 points. The second-order federated update converges in only a few rounds. The resulting sparsity compresses the stored model, the per-sample inference cost, and the server-to-client broadcast by a comparable factor. These results demonstrate the practical value of sparse readouts for edge computing and IoT deployments.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.21720: Federated LLM unlearning addresses targeted knowledge removal when forget and retain data remain distributed across private clients and are inaccessible to the server. The resulting locally trained adapters encode conflicting objectives, making their aggregation fundamentally different from conventional federated optimization. A key failure mode is magnitude explosion, whereby unnormalized cross-client aggregation increases the merged update magnitude and degrades retained utility under stronger unlearning. We propose FIRM (Fisher-Informed Retention Merging), a single-round framework for stable and retention-aware server-side aggregation. FIRM uses client-local Fisher statistics as a unified sensitivity signal to construct a Fisher-normalized base merge and impose explicit control over retain-sensitive parameters. Its second-order retention projection admits a unique minimum-distance solution, while the corresponding dual scales with the number of retain clients rather than the model dimension. Experiments across WMDP, TOFU, and MUSE-HP using Zephyr-7B and Llama-3-8B show utility gains at comparable forgetting on WMDP and MUSE-HP, with metric-dependent trade-offs on TOFU. Controlled comparisons support benefits of the combined base merge and additional retention correction at selected operating points.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.21295: Federated minimax problems, such as distributionally robust optimization and adversarial training, include an inner maximization variable built from each client's local data. These variables differ in meaning and dimension from one client to the next, so averaging them across clients, as standard federated minimax methods do, is ill-posed. We therefore study a federated minimax problem where the minimization variable $\mathbf{x}$ is shared and aggregated, while each client retains the maximization variable $\mathbf{y}_i$ (personalized). Because these applications constrain $\mathbf{y}_i$ to a compact convex set, we analyze projected ascent directly. We show that, in the nonconvex-concave regime, this projected personalized scheme attains the standard sublinear rate. In the nonconvex-PL regime, however, it hits a stepsize-invariant noise floor due to stochastic $\mathbf{y}_i$ updates. To mitigate this, we propose VR-SGDA, incorporating a variance-reduced ascent step where each client maintains a private variable snapshot. By evaluating current and snapshot gradients on the same sample, the constant variance is replaced by a vanishing drift under a two-timescale regime. VR-SGDA eliminates the noise floor, attaining sublinear leading rates while preserving personalization and projection. Experiments on subpopulation-robustness and NLP adversarial training confirm both the worst-group robustness benefits and the two-timescale tracking mechanism.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.21194: Existing federated intelligence paradigms primarily focus on how models are trained or aggregated, while overlooking a more fundamental question: \textbf{what information should leave the client?} Existing methods often share model updates that users cannot easily inspect, or data representations that may reveal sensitive information. Moreover, generating these representations can be computationally expensive for resource-constrained clients. We observe that image classification does not require all the visual details needed to reconstruct the original image. This suggests that clients could share less information while preserving task performance. However, learning what to preserve is challenging when the server cannot access raw client data. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{FedPix}, which learns to share compact, visually inspectable images instead of model updates or intermediate features. The key idea is to use the shared representations themselves to learn what information should be preserved and what can be discarded. By balancing task utility and reconstruction resistance, FedPix enables the server to improve the representations without accessing raw client data, while keeping client-side computation lightweight. Extensive experiments on BloodMNIST, CIFAR-10, FashionMNIST, and MNIST demonstrate that FedPix achieves strong reconstruction resistance, with reconstruction PSNR as low as 6.87~dB and synthetic PSNR as low as 6.74~dB. Meanwhile, FedPix reduces client runtime by up to 96.0\% (from 1223~s to 49~s on CIFAR-10), while maintaining competitive classification accuracy of 99.18\% on MNIST, 89.97\% on FashionMNIST, 82.24\% on BloodMNIST, and 65.63\% on CIFAR-10.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.21547: Federated learning (FL) is increasingly used to adapt a pretrained, centrally fine-tuned model to data that remain on user devices, beyond training a model from scratch. In this report, prepared for the 4th Federated Machine Learning International Summer School, we study the privacy and integrity of this approach with a reproducible pipeline. An ImageNet-pretrained MobileNetV4-Conv-Small model is fine-tuned centrally on ten Quick, Draw! classes (97.50% test accuracy) and then adapted with head-only FedAvg over ten non-IID clients, which raises client training accuracy from 90.34% to 91.49% while preserving global accuracy. We evaluate four adversarial scenarios. First, from a single one-step client update, an honest-but-curious server recovers the complete private label set, but its reconstructions follow class prototypes rather than the private drawings (mean SSIM 0.130). Second, from a one-round FedAvg aggregate, label-count recovery falls from 87.5% with one client to 75.0% with five and ten clients, below the 80.0% of an uninformed uniform guess. Third, under FedAvg, a backdoor injected by 30%, 50%, and 100% of the clients reaches an attack success rate (ASR) of 21.9%, 31.3%, and 54.7% at a cost of at most 0.8 percentage points of clean accuracy, whereas label flipping is effective only when most of the source-class data are relabeled. Fourth, FLTrust with a root set retained from centralized fine-tuning lowers the backdoor ASR to 1.8% and 4.0% at 30% and 50% malicious clients and the label-flipping ASR from 12.6% to 0.8% without measurable clean-accuracy loss, but provides no protection when every client is malicious. The report closes with a live session in which participants draw, fine-tune, and poison the model through Indigma's FedMaestro orchestrator. Code and executed notebooks, runnable on Google Colab, are at https://github.com/Indigma-Innovations/fl-summer-school.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.22584: Connected vehicles train a driving model through federated learning (FL) and drive with it, so a faulty contribution often surfaces only as a delayed symptom on the road. Federated unlearning (FU) assumes that a removal request names what to forget. A symptom names no vehicle or round, and aggregation has already spread its cause across the fleet. We propose \underline{A}ggregation-\underline{T}ime \underline{O}perational-evidence \underline{N}eutralization of \underline{E}ffects (\method{}), which makes unlearning a term of the FL aggregation rule. \method{} projects everyday driving errors and reported symptoms onto a subspace spanned by recent global increments. It propagates the surviving effect of every contribution with curvature estimated from these increments and scores all contributions in one backward pass. A two-tier correction suppresses suspected effects in every round and eliminates confirmed ones after a one-round probe. We prove that backward scoring matches forward scoring and that the elimination is exact when training is flat outside the subspace. On three driving datasets, \method{} leaves 43\% to 61\% less residual harm than the strongest baseline in eight of nine settings while staying within 0.36 points of full retraining in utility.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.22626: Advanced persistent threats (APTs) are a major concern in federated learning (FL) deployments in critical sectors such as healthcare, and finance. Traditional defense mechanisms fail to contain APTs due to their intermittent attacking behavior. This paper addresses a specific type of APT called covert model poisoning (CMP) where the attacker intermittently injects poisoned model updates in a covert manner. The interaction between the FL server and a CMP attacker is modeled as an imperfect repeated game where both players cannot observe each other's actions. A novel adversarial search algorithm called StratFL is designed alongside novel belief update algorithms at both the server and adversary. Experiments are designed using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets to evaluate and compare StratFL's performance against state-of-the-art methods. Empirical convergence of belief update algorithms is demonstrated across various security vignettes. At the same time, StratFL is found to exhibit an improved accuracy of 10% compared to state-of-the-art methods.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.24013: Peer-to-peer collaborative learning is an emerging distributed deep learning paradigm that eliminates the need for a central aggregator and disseminator, avoiding the single-point-of-failure and bottleneck issues they can bring. Many such approaches use parameter averaging, requiring clients to have homogeneous model architectures, whereas others use knowledge distillation as an alternative while leaning on shared public data or centralized control infrastructure. Many of these approaches also make a one-size-fits-all assumption, i.e., jointly training a single, globally optimal solution for all clients, when in reality, clients' underlying data distributions might differ such that a globally optimal solution may not be locally optimal for all clients. To enable collaborative learning in environments with both model architecture and data distribution heterogeneity, we present SPADE-KD -- a fully decentralized model distillation framework that optimizes collaboration towards personalized rather than global performance. SPADE-KD leverages two mechanisms -- adaptive distillation and utility-driven peer selection. Adaptive distillation modulates the strength of each incoming model transfer by the performance advantage of the incoming model compared to the native model measured by their task losses, such that a client will distill more aggressively from incoming models that outperform it on its own local data. Utility-driven peer selection uses the loss-informed utility derived from adaptive distillation to rank prospective partners, focusing on exchanges that measurably improve the local model while suppressing low-utility transfers. Using federated classification tasks, we demonstrate that SPADE-KD consistent outperforms naive decentralized distillation with lower loss and faster convergence and that its individual components are more effective together than independently.
arxiv:2610.21969: The convergence of communication and computation, empowered by artificial intelligence (AI) enhanced capabilities, emerges as a key enabler for realizing the promising functionalities of the sixth-generation of communication systems (6G). To this end, this paper investigates an AI-native, robust network, where multiple base stations (BSs) simultaneously serve several extended reality (XR) devices. The paper then presents an innovative distributed deep learning-based approach to simultaneously manage the transmit and computing powers, and computation allocation, amidst uncertainties in both channel and computing states information. Under such an interference network scenario, the paper proposes a robust approach for minimizing the worst-case delay across the served XR devices, subject to computation and power constraints. The paper leverages a deep neural network (DNN) that can be trained either centrally or in a federated manner to map estimated channels and computation requirements to optimized resource allocations per BS. During training, uncertainty samples, reflecting both channel and computing estimation errors, are injected after the DNN output to account for such joint uncertainties. Our results validate the enhanced robust delay performance and scalability of joint uncertainty injection as compared to uncertainty-agnostic methods and state-of-the-art benchmarks, with federated learning-based solutions achieving near-centralized performance while enhancing efficiency, privacy, and adaptability.
arxiv:2610.20661: Big data analytics supports modern intelligent systems, but model complexity and limited transparency can undermine interpretability, trust, and security in decision-making. This paper presents the Hybrid DeepXAI Fusion Network, a deep learning framework that integrates temporal, relational, and contextual features with explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) mechanisms. The architecture combines one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D-CNNs) for temporal feature extraction, Transformer encoders for contextual modeling, and graph neural networks (GNNs) for inter-feature dependency analysis. An attention-based fusion mechanism integrates these representations. Class Activation Mapping (CAM) and an explanation loss are incorporated to improve interpretability and explanation consistency. The framework is designed for deployment in a federated cloud architecture, using homomorphic encryption and blockchain-based auditing to support data privacy and accountability. Experimental evaluations across healthcare, finance, and energy datasets report 98.42% accuracy, 97.9% precision, 98.1% recall, and a 98.0% F1-score, outperforming the evaluated CNN-LSTM, Transformer-only, and XGBoost baselines. Under projected gradient descent (PGD) adversarial perturbations, the model reportedly retains accuracy above 91.5%. Scalability experiments report throughput of 80,000 messages per second with latency below 200 milliseconds. These results suggest that the proposed framework has potential for interpretable and secure cloud-based decision-support systems.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.20264: Client-level fair federated learning, in the form of $q$-fair federated learning ($q$-FFL), agnostic federated learning, or tilted empirical risk minimization, has emerged as an attractive solution to equalize utility across heterogeneous clients. This paradigm grants high-loss clients greater relative influence, while a central server aggregates their loss-weighted updates into a single shared model. Yet, the Byzantine robustness of $q$-fair federated learning has been largely neglected, leaving the server unable to tell legitimate fairness-induced amplification from malicious update scaling. To address this critical gap, we formalize the problem of Byzantine-robust $q$-fair federated learning under an \emph{update-only interface}, in which the server observes nothing but the fairness-scaled client updates. Our analysis under shared class-conditional label skew shows that fairness scaling preserves the nonnegative class-mixture structure of honest updates, while replacing their unit-sum constraint by a client-dependent radial scale. Moving beyond magnitude-based screening, we show that this warped geometry supplies two complementary tests, one radial and one structural, that a single norm cannot provide. We then introduce FUSE, a structure-aware robust aggregator that uses a small trusted labeled dataset for coefficient recovery, scale and cone-consistency screening, and post-screening step-size control. Across four benchmarks and seven Byzantine attacks, FUSE improves seed-wise worst-attack accuracy over the strongest baseline on each benchmark by 3.9--30.1 percentage points, while largely preserving the influence of the high-loss honest clients that fairness is meant to protect.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.20530: Open Radio Access Networks (O-RANs) bring intelligence to disaggregated RANs through virtualized platforms and open interfaces, but the stringent latency budgets of the RAN Intelligent Controller (RIC) and heterogeneous traffic conditions make real-time deployment costly. Centralized learning is ill-suited to the RIC due to its computational burden, timing constraints, and communication overhead, motivating Federated Learning (FL) as a distributed alternative. We formulate FL in O-RAN as a Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Program (MINLP) that minimizes communication cost and learning time under heterogeneity in User Equipment (UE) compute, traffic, and channel conditions, and decompose it into a UE Assignment (UA) subproblem and a Computation and Bandwidth Allocation (CBA) subproblem. We then propose FedRIC, a heterogeneity-aware FL framework combining compressed gradient descent, slice-aware resource allocation, and multilevel hierarchical aggregation. Experiments show that FedRIC outperforms FedCOM, FedAvg, and QFedAvg in convergence rate, communication cost, and latency.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.20075: Federated learning over decentralized networks inherently trades off the suppression of local finite-sample noise through collaboration against the bias that collaboration introduces between heterogeneous nodes. We study this tension by performing a large-dimensional analysis of Generalized Total Variation Minimization with least-squares models. Using tools from random matrix theory, we show that Lipschitz observations of the global GTVMin solution concentrate in large dimensions, universally for any underlying network structure. We provide exact analytic expressions for the asymptotically precise performance under both i.i.d. and non-i.i.d. Gaussian mixture distributions on a fixed network. For the latter, these expressions quantify how regularization balances local adaptation against collaboration. Our theoretical results are confirmed by experiments on synthetic and real-world data.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.19808: Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) based on deep learning often fail to detect attack classes that are absent from training data, limiting their robustness against zero-day threats. This property called transferability across attack classes, remains underexplored especially in federated learning (FL) settings where data heterogeneity and client drift pose additional challenges. Prior work (TabFIDS) showed that FedAvg combined with bootstrapping and temporal averaging improves transferability for cross-device NIDS. In this paper, we explore whether other federated optimizers can do better. We compare two optimizers inspired by FedAdam and FedProx against the FedAvg baseline on the CIC-IDS 2017 dataset using an 11-client federated setup, sweep 10 hyperparameter configurations, and contrast two data-balancing strategies: bootstrapping and SMOTE. Using the count of client pairs whose transferred-model accuracy exceeds 70% as our primary metric (following TabFIDS), the proximal optimizer with a strong regularization term yields 48 transferable pairs versus 42 for FedAvg, while the adaptive optimizer with an aggressive server learning rate yields 46 pairs. SMOTE improves per-pair accuracy over bootstrapping but reduces breadth, revealing a depth-vs-breadth trade-off: high accuracy on a few client pairs versus moderate accuracy across most. These results indicate that the choice of federated optimizer, the rule by which client updates are regularized and aggregated into the global model, is very important for federated NIDS.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.19968: Federated fine-tuning enables large language models (LLMs) to learn collaboratively from distributed client data, but malicious client updates can compromise global model safety. As federated tasks evolve, changing malicious update patterns challenge the ability of existing defenses to maintain reliable risk detection over time. To address this challenge, we propose Safe-FCL, a framework integrating continual risk awareness with fine-grained safety aggregation for federated continual learning of LLMs. Specifically, the Continual Risk Awareness (CRA) mechanism learns emerging risk patterns across sequential tasks and constrains detector updates using a protective subspace derived from historical features, mitigating forgetting of previously learned malicious patterns while adapting to new risks. To translate risk awareness into aggregation-level safety control, the Fine-Grained Safety Aggregation (FGSA) mechanism combines client-level risk assessments from CRA with module-level deviations from historical update behavior to adaptively regulate aggregation contributions, suppressing potentially malicious updates while minimizing unnecessary restrictions on benign updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Safe-FCL outperforms current SOTA methods, improving global-model Rule and MD-Judge scores in federated continual learning by 0.41% and 0.64%, respectively, while increasing average risk recognition accuracy by 2.01%.
arxiv:2610.20753: Large language models (LLMs) trained on vast amounts of data have demonstrated impressive performance over a range of tasks, but future performance gains will require increasing amounts of data and compute. Federated Learning (FL) facilitates training on decentralized private data, but client resource limitations can make training impractical, particularly as model sizes continue to expand. These resource constraints make the assumption of a shared server-client architecture impractical. Model heterogeneous FL offers a promising alternative by adapting model size to client capabilities; however, previous work is limited to the pre-training setting, and conclusions on sub-network selection do not necessarily hold for fine-tuning. Furthermore, prior approaches create client sub-networks without considering their unique data distributions, thereby overlooking the opportunity to tailor sub-network architecture to local data. Motivated by evidence that attention heads exhibit task dependency within layer defined feature spaces, we propose Optimal Hydra, a transformer based heterogeneous FL framework for fine-tuning that combines global layer selection with client specific attention head selection, aligned with local data distributions. Optimal Hydra makes explicit use of client data to produce client-specific sub-networks we call Hydra-nets. To our knowledge, this is the first model heterogeneous FL approach tailored to LLM fine-tuning. Experiments on three datasets show significant improvements over baseline methods while also reducing local resource demands.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.18430: Federated fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) allows multiple clients to collaboratively adapt models without sharing raw data, offering strong privacy benefits. However, this setting is highly vulnerable to backdoor attacks, in which malicious clients manipulate their updates to induce targeted behaviors while maintaining normal performance on benign inputs. In this work, we make a key observation specific to federated LLM fine-tuning: malicious clients tend to exhibit strong consistency in their model updates, whereas benign clients produce more diverse and dispersed updates. This structural difference is not well captured by existing defense methods, which typically rely on direct anomaly detection in high-dimensional parameter space and therefore struggle in the presence of entangled LLM updates. Motivated by this observation, we propose FedGraph, a graph-based aggregation framework that explicitly models relationships among client updates. By representing clients as nodes in a dynamically constructed graph and extracting structural features that characterize their relative positions and interactions, FedGraph derives compact client representations that effectively separate malicious and benign behaviors. These representations are then used to identify and suppress malicious contributions during aggregation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedGraph significantly improves backdoor defense. It consistently reduces attack success rates to below 10% while achieving high detection accuracy (95.5% on average) and a low false positive rate (2.33%), substantially outperforming existing federated learning defenses.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.18640: In Intelligent Transport Systems, protecting vulnerable road users, specifically pedestrians, is a paramount challenge. The present work contributes to this field, putting forth a distributed architecture in which vehicles connected to the cellular infrastructure collect pedestrians' trajectories and fine-tune a foundation model for pedestrian trajectory forecasting via federated training. A server positioned at the edge of the cellular network is responsible for aggregating the local model's parameters from the vehicles and updating the global model's parameters. To reduce radio resource utilization, Low-Rank Adaptation is proposed; to decrease both the number and the size of updates, an increase in the number of training rounds performed by the vehicles per communication round is put forth. A novel figure of merit is then introduced to quantify the use of radio resources dedicated to Vehicle-to-Infrastructure communications as required by the federated solution. The proposed scheme delivers excellent prediction accuracy while significantly reducing the communication cost compared to alternative federated training methods. This shows that combining fine-tuning, Low-Rank Adaptation, and a reduction of the communication periodicity between the vehicles and the edge server is key to enabling a distributed approach to trajectory prediction in vehicular environments.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.18771: International challenges have become the standard for developing and benchmarking biomedical image analysis methods using centralized multi-institutional data. Federated learning (FL) describes a paradigm-shift on multi-institutional collaborations, where models are trained across institutions while their data are always retained locally. The Federated Tumor Segmentation (FeTS) challenge, first held in 2021, was the first challenge dedicated to FL in medical imaging and editions in 2022 and 2024 pushed the frontiers of real-world method validation. FeTS++ 2027 returns after a two-year gap with a substantially larger and more diverse cohort, and with the two "pluses" that name the challenge: an official classification task alongside segmentation, and a move of the infrastructure to NVIDIA FLARE (NVFlare). Built on the clinically acquired, multi-institutional multi-parametric MRI data of the BraTS 2025 Lighthouse challenge, FeTS++ spans gliomas and meningiomas across patient cohorts from institutions in North America, Europe, Asia, and Africa, and focuses on ranking submitted methodological approaches according to their model utility and an efficiency-aware score. Task 1 asks participants to find the best strategy for aggregating knowledge from per-institution segmentation models, while Task 2 asks them to distinguish glioma from meningioma under the same federated protocol, in which the entity label is heavily confounded with the site of origin.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.17551: The dominant barrier to running large clinical language models at the point of care is not arithmetic throughput but graphics memory: consumer GPUs cap at 4-16 GB, while the working set of a 27-billion-parameter model in 4-bit precision is 17-25 GB. We argue that the edge node should be treated as capacity-enabled (system RAM) rather than compute-limited (GPU VRAM), and we test this on commodity hardware. Using an INT4 build of a 27B open model as an architecture-faithful stand-in for a 27B medical model, we measure the memory footprint, inference latency, energy, and federated communication cost of a fully CPU-based pipeline driven by synthetic Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) prompts. On two independent consumer machines (a desktop-class machine with 67 GB of RAM and a 6 GB GPU, and a mobile workstation with 34 GB of RAM and a 4 GB GPU) the model loads entirely into system RAM (37% and 60% utilization, respectively) while both GPUs are out-of-memory before the first step. Inference runs at overnight-batch speed (0.6-2.4 tokens/s for the 27B model), and federated fine-tuning would transmit only a 22.6 MB low-rank adapter, a 99.96% reduction over full weights. The capacity result is independent of CPU microarchitecture, RAM size, operating system, and GPU. We further identify an open, CPU- and NPU-optimized inference runtime as the natural production path for this approach, indicating a privacy-preserving and broadly deployable route for on-premises clinical AI. All data is synthetic; this is a research artifact and not a medical device.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.17621: We propose FedLoRD, a personalized federated learning (PFL) method based on the low-rank structure of the differences between the global and personalized model parameters. PFL is a branch of federated learning that aims to learn models tailored to the local data of each client under biased local data distributions. In its local training, each client learns a personalized model by regularizing the difference between its model parameters and the global ones sent from the server. The regularization function needs to be designed with priors on the model parameter difference; however, the existing PFL methods rely on empirical choices (e.g., $\ell_1$- and $\ell_2$-norms), which do not take into account the actual characteristics of the difference. The resulting mismatch of priors can lead to suboptimal personalized models. To address this issue, we propose a PFL method whose regularizer is built on an observed characteristic of the model parameter differences: they are approximately low-rank at every layer. In our method, we first formulate a local training problem with nuclear norm regularization on the layer-wise differences. We further rewrite this problem via the factorized representation of the nuclear norm so that it can be efficiently solved by a plain stochastic gradient descent method. Image classification experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that FedLoRD outperforms several existing PFL methods.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.17523: With recent developments in Artificial Intelligence (AI), the adoption of distributed learning paradigms such as Federated Learning (FL) has emerged. In simple terms, FL enables multiple entities to collaboratively train AI models without sharing local data. The FL paradigm is particularly valuable in privacy-sensitive settings, such as financial services, because it enables institutions to collaboratively improve fraud-detection models while keeping sensitive transaction data local. However, FL schemes are prone to security vulnerabilities, where malicious clients can poison local data or model updates and degrade the global model, and hence the performance of the resulting model might be affected. Therefore, in this work, we propose Enhanced Detective, a dual-stage robust aggregation strategy that combines Median Absolute Deviation (MAD), distance-based update filtering, and FedMedian aggregation. Experiments on an imbalanced credit card dataset evaluate targeted label-flipping and weight-scaling attacks over 50 communication rounds. With 40% malicious clients, Enhanced Detective achieves an AUPRC of 0.796 and a Recall of 0.847.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.17913: Distributed learning with multiple local steps reduces communication but aggravates drift, and its practical performance often depends on carefully tuned hyperparameters under heterogeneous data and communication constraints. At the same time, recent Muon-type optimizers suggest that constraining updates within suitable norm balls provides a simple way to encode geometric priors into optimization. In this work, we propose NBCLT (Norm-Ball Clipped Local Training), a unified local-training framework for both federated learning (FL) and decentralized learning (DL). NBCLT combines a predict-and-correct local update rule with Euclidean projections onto flexible norm balls, thereby performing norm-ball clipping under flexible update geometries while retaining a simple implementation. In FL, its problem-parameter-free regime achieves $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-2})$ communication complexity and $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-4})$ total stochastic-gradient complexity without assuming bounded heterogeneity, when the per-round local-computation budget is scaled appropriately with the horizon. In DL, NBCLT is compatible with both static and time-varying mixing and preserves these accuracy exponents under the analogous computation scaling, up to fixed network constants and an additive initialization cost.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.19077: Quantum federated learning trains a quantum neural network (QNN) across nodes that hold quantum data, such as the states of quantum sensors. To forget data, unlearning methods for quantum models replay them, and federated unlearning from stored updates removes whole nodes only. Quantum data cannot be replayed, since a state is consumed when measured and cannot be cloned. We propose Shadow-based Data Erasure (SHADE), in which each node records a classical shadow of every training state, a few randomized single-qubit measurements taken at training time. The gradient and curvature of a QNN on a state are expectations of observables, so SHADE estimates them for the forget data from the shadows at any later parameters and removes their effect by a federated Newton correction. Only classical estimates cross the network. We prove that the shadow size needed for a target unlearning error grows exponentially in the size of the backward light cone of the measured observable and not in the number of qubits. In simulation with 50 nodes and on edge boards, SHADE matches the forget accuracy of retraining within 0.5 points, without replay and in under 0.2 s.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.16425: In real-world scenarios, industrial processes can span multiple factories and goods are often produced at multiple sites, leading to a shared yet non-identical distribution of data across locations. To address this, we propose two federated approaches for i) combining existing coresets (Double Subsampling) and ii) creating new coresets (Federated Subsampling) in a distributed anomaly detection setting. In particular, we adapt the memory bank based PatchCore algorithm to a federated setting, resulting in increased cold-start performance, resilience to domain- and sensor-shift, and resilience to unreliable actor participation, a common problem in classical, network based federated learning strategies.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.16987: Multimodal decentralized learning enables collaboration across heterogeneous edge devices without sharing raw data, but differing modality sets create coupled computation and communication bottlenecks. Multimodal agents support cross-modal alignment while training more model components and sharing bandwidth across multiple modality overlays. Under bandwidth limits, these agents can become hot spots: transfers miss aggregation windows, and their updates become stale or underrepresented, degrading worst-agent accuracy. Asynchrony removes global blocking but does not by itself coordinate local cross-modal interaction with timely peer-update exchange. We present MODAIC (Modality-Decoupled Asynchrony with Interleaved Coordination), a wait-free system that coordinates local modality progress, peer-to-peer update delivery, and aggregation under heterogeneous compute and bandwidth. Hierarchical asynchrony lets modalities progress independently while enforcing reciprocal feature exchange; load-aware update fetching overlaps training with communication, limits concurrent serving load, and reuses late arrivals; and consensus-aware peer selection uses lightweight metadata to account for update availability, peer participation, and loss similarity without active probing. We implement MODAIC as a containerized multi-agent framework and evaluate it on local and cross-region cloud testbeds. Across AVE and KU-HAR, MODAIC improves average accuracy and multimodal worst-agent performance. On AVE at 200 Mbps per agent, it improves multimodal worst-agent accuracy by 11.0 percentage points at 1000 seconds over the strongest baseline. On the cloud testbed, it reduces time-to-accuracy by up to 30%. Ablations show that simpler load-balancing and delayed-aggregation variants leave a worst-agent accuracy gap, and stress tests show tolerance to WAN variability and partial tracker unavailability.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.16872: In Operational Technology (OT) environments, Federated Learning (FL) is increasingly adopted to train Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) without sharing raw operational data across facilities. However, model updates may still leak sensitive information about industrial processes, creating privacy risks that remain largely invisible within current OT security architectures. Existing reference models, including the Purdue hierarchy, do not explicitly represent the FL learning lifecycle, making privacy leakage difficult to observe and evaluate. To address this gap, we introduce the ML Plane, a novel architectural abstraction that integrates FL workflows within OT systems, enabling visibility of learning-related information flows that are not explicitly represented in traditional OT architectures. Building on the proposed ML Plane, we outline a privacy auditing framework for FL-enabled OT systems. The framework uses Federated Membership Inference Attacks (FedMIA) as an initial assessment mechanism and is being instantiated within a Smart Grid testbed to support the future evaluation of privacy risks under realistic OT deployment constraints.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.17265: Federated learning allows hospitals to train a shared mortality model without pooling their records, but published comparisons of aggregation strategies rarely control the evaluation protocol. This study compared seven strategies (FedAvg, FedProx, SCAFFOLD, FedAdagrad, FedAdam, FedYogi and FedCluster) on two federations built with one pipeline: 12 care units of a hospital in MIMIC-IV and 49 hospitals in eICU-CRD. Each strategy was tuned and selected on validation data by the same rule, and every comparison was repeated across 10 seeds with Friedman and Holm-corrected tests. SCAFFOLD ranked first in both federations (AUC-ROC 0.886 and 0.819) and in 17 of 18 variants, but its margin over the runner-up never exceeded 0.008, and a control sharing its local optimizer attributed most of its margin over FedAvg to drift correction. On the multi-hospital federation, federated training matched centralized training. In the care-unit federation, three protocol choices changed discrimination by more than the choice of strategy did: discharge-coded predictors (+0.038 in AUC-ROC), client-level SMOTE (up to -0.074), and evaluating the last instead of the best validation round (up to -0.084). Platt scaling on validation data repaired the risks distorted by imbalance corrections without loss of discrimination. Studies should therefore fix the protocol before ranking algorithms.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.15543: We study federated learning from continuously arriving data: each client samples from its own distribution, these distributions drift over time, and the server must track the minimizer of the clients' weighted average loss. Clients are not alike as they collect data at different rates, with different noise, and change at different speeds. The main question is how much history should each one keep? A single shared window must serve every client at once, and so makes a fast-changing client carry the sampling noise of a slow, nearly stationary one. We give each client a memory of its own, sized to that client's noise, arrival rate, and drift, and refresh it by restarted accelerated method that starts from a common point. The tracking error is then bounded by \[ R\left(\sum_m w_m^{3/2}\,σ_m\sqrt{γ_m/λ_m}\right)^{2/3}, \] for clients with weight $w_m$, noise $σ_m$, arrival rate $λ_m$, and drift rate $γ_m$ on a domain of diameter $R$. This is never worse than what any common window can achieve, and strictly better whenever noise and drift are spread unevenly across clients. A lower bound that puts different groups of clients on different drift clocks shows this quantity is the right one. The two bounds agree up to a constant whenever the clients occupy boundedly many refresh scales, and in general differ only by the sixth root of the number of scales. Experiments show the gain comes from the memory rather than from the solver: it persists across accelerated, stochastic-gradient, and one-step methods, and against a separately tuned common-memory baseline.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.13311: Inside a federated learning system a participant can quietly study the shared model and learn about others' private data. The usual defense, differential privacy, often adds so much noise that the model is no longer worth training. In cross-silo FL, where participants are a few accountable organizations and the server is trusted, we ask whether the server can instead interrogate clients. Each round it sends a secret challenge batch and asks every client to return a checksum of the gradient that batch induces, together with a timing. A client that mutated the model state, as an active generative-adversarial-network discriminator attacker does, returns a wrong checksum. We make this checksum robust to benign cross-platform floating-point non-determinism with a quantized fingerprint compared under a small tolerance. It flags two distinct active attacks at a true-positive rate of $1.0$ with no false positives on the checksum axis, stable across the fingerprint's parameters and up to $50$ clients at malicious ratios to $40\%$, for $32\,\mathrm{ms}$ of server work and $4.35\,\mathrm{kB}$ per response. Against a purely passive attacker the only signal is timing, and it is not robust: a cohort-relative test detects only in low-jitter conditions while a false-positive-free per-client baseline is blind, so no configuration delivers both. An attacker that answers the challenge on an untouched copy of the model while tampering with a replica evades the audit entirely. Therefore the checksum is a reliable in-band signal against attackers that do not decouple the audited computation from the attacked one, and it composes with differential privacy, whose accuracy cost we quantify on Texas100, rather than replacing it.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.13508: Federated learning (FL) seeks to optimize a shared global model from decentralized client data. While effective for average performance, this process can produce unfair performance across clients, particularly under statistically heterogeneous data distributions. Existing fairness-aware and multi-objective FL methods address this through client re-weighting, gradient correction, or common-descent formulations, but often change the global optimization direction or treat client objectives symmetrically. We propose FedPCD, a priority-constrained federated optimization framework that separates the global optimization objective from client protection. FedPCD preserves the conventional federated aggregate as the primary objective, while allowing only the minimum correction necessary to meet client performance constraints. Across heterogeneous FL benchmarks, FedPCD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving the highest global accuracy across all configurations and leading worst-10% client accuracy in nearly all. FedPCD further preserves competitive trade-offs between global accuracy and client performance variability. Beyond this trade-off, FedPCD demonstrates faster empirical convergence, reaching matching or superior performance in substantially fewer communication rounds.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.13631: Fault diagnosis in asset-intensive industries requires multiclass models trained on noisy, sensitive data collected across geographically distributed client sites. Federated learning enables collaborative training without centralizing data, but most approaches do not provide formal privacy guarantees for individual records stored at client sites and can degrade under label noise. To address these limitations, we develop a differentially private, distributionally robust framework for federated multiclass classification that provides sample-level privacy for records stored at each client. We build on a federated Wasserstein distributionally robust multiclass objective with the Crammer-Singer loss, solved using an Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM)-based algorithm. To protect the released client updates, our method injects calibrated Gaussian noise into the proximal linearized client updates of both the local model and the local distributionally robust variable before aggregation at the central server, and we quantify the cumulative privacy loss using the moments accountant. We provide per-round sample-level $(ε,δ)$-differential privacy guarantees and an overall composed privacy guarantee across all training rounds, together with convergence results and an explicit privacy-utility tradeoff. Experiments on simulated industrial fault data and UCI benchmark datasets show that our method outperforms differentially private federated empirical risk minimization and stochastic gradient descent baselines in most tested settings, with the largest gains under strong privacy-induced noise.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.12907: Federated vision-language models (FedVLMs) represent one of the emerging frontiers of machine learning, aiming to integrate federated learning within the fine-tuning pipelines of vision-language models (VLMs). In this work, we introduce BLEND, a new framework designed to jointly enhance the personalization and generalization capabilities of FedVLMs. BLEND proposes a selective VLM parameter fine-tuning and aggregation strategy that consists of (i) global vision and text adapters shared across clients, and (ii) a personalized vision projection adapter tailored to each client. BLEND further introduces a novel loss function that blends the outputs of the global and personalized adapters to achieve personalization, while simultaneously promoting generalization through a principled anchor design implemented via the projection heads of the zero-shot VLM. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BLEND consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, highlighting its ability to effectively balance personalization and generalization across diverse system settings. (Code is available at: https://github.com/payamsiabd/BLEND.git)
10.48550/arxiv.2610.13717: Federated clustering can support applications such as patient stratification across hospitals and customer segmentation across distributed financial datasets. Responsible AI calls for fair representation of demographic groups and support for data deletion, motivated in part by rights such as the GDPR's right to erasure. These goals interact: deleting records can change the balance between groups and alter the clustering of the remaining population. We study exact machine unlearning for federated socially fair $k$-means, whose objective is to minimize the largest group-average squared distance to the nearest center. Our approach keeps separate local summaries for each group, so summaries at unaffected institutions remain valid as global fairness weights change. For two groups, we prove an initialization approximation guarantee independent of client group proportions under ideal sampling, and we show that same-seed replay reproduces retraining exactly. Reuse pays off most when a whole client withdraws: across three datasets, replay is $35.8\times$ faster than retraining for the initialization-only model and remains $2.4\times$ and $1.7\times$ faster with one and two fair-refinement rounds, which improve worst-group cost. For individual record deletions, gains are modest (about $1.06\times$), and certifying cached assignments can cost more than it saves. These results map where exact unlearning can profitably reuse computation. Code and reproducibility materials are available at https://github.com/arareddy/mufsc.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.12909: Accurate charging load forecasting is essential for the reliability and efficiency of the Internet of Electric Vehicles (IoEV), yet it is challenging on two fronts: charging demand is highly stochastic, and the data collected by distributed sensors is privacy-sensitive. Although federated learning (FL) preserves data privacy, collaborative training still remains vulnerable to an honest-but-curious server that can invert shared model updates to reconstruct private data. To address both data volatility and privacy concerns, we propose SecFD-FL, a frequency-decoupled federated learning framework for IoEV comprising: 1) a dual-stream gated recurrent unit (GRU) network that separately models short-term and long-term charging load volatility, and 2) a lightweight secure aggregation layer for privacy preservation. Specifically, the secure aggregation layer employs a zero-sum additive masking protocol that perturbs each client's upload with high-variance noise, preventing the server from reconstructing private data while preserving the exact aggregate. Extensive experiments have been conducted on both EV-level and charging station-level using real datasets. The experiment results show that SecFD-FL reduces global RMSE by up to 60% over centralized baselines, achieving Jain's fairness up to 0.991 across clients, and reduces DLG-attack reconstruction correlation by 8 times to 15 times relative to FedAvg -- all with no additional per-round communication cost beyond a one-time key exchange.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.12916: Existing governance approaches in decentralized financial networks rely on manual review processes conducted by human committees, which introduces subjective bias, creates a scalability bottleneck under high network volume, and fails to capture complex behavioural patterns and evolving network dynamics. To address these limitations, we propose \name, a federated learning-based pairwise ranking framework in which multiple institutions collaboratively train a ranking model without sharing their private transaction data. This collaborative learning enables the model to capture network-wide behavioural patterns that signify strong network participation and directly contribute to the network effect, including diversity of counterparties, usage of multiple applications, and frequency of transactions. The proposed system ranks providers based on the authenticity of their actions, promoting genuine contributors and demoting those exhibiting suspicious behaviour. We evaluate \name\ on a real-world blockchain transaction dataset. Results demonstrate that the federated approach achieves ranking performance modestly below the centralized baseline (NDCG@15: $\approx$0.87 vs.\ $\approx$0.92) while preserving data privacy and matching its ranking stability (Kendall $τ$: $\approx$0.70 for both regimes), producing reliable governance decisions, including provider promotion and demotion (648 and 39 unique providers, respectively), without requiring centralized access to sensitive transaction data.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.14289: LLM watermarking has emerged as a promising approach for detecting downstream model misuse in centralized settings, but extending it to federated learning (FL) presents unique challenges. In particular, FL systems often rely on strong robust aggregators to defend against poisoning attacks. We empirically show that a malicious server can exploit these same aggregators as effective watermark-removal mechanisms during training, causing representative existing LLM watermarking methods to fail detection in the final model. To address this limitation, we formalize the problem as a constrained optimization task and propose CamoMark, an aggregator-agnostic watermarking scheme for embedding robust watermarks in FL. CamoMark optimizes watermarked updates to become inliers, maintaining bounded deviation from the distribution of clean updates, while preserving sufficient watermark signal for reliable detection. Evaluated on Qwen fine-tuned on the Alpaca dataset, CamoMark achieves a detection confidence of $p$-value $= 1.82\times10^{-2}$ using only 3.3% watermarked data. The watermark also remains robust to a range of post-training removal attacks, including continued fine-tuning on clean data, pruning, and model distillation. At higher watermark ratios, detection confidence improves substantially, reaching $p$-value $= 5.11\times10^{-11}$ at a 13.3% watermark ratio.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.14268: The scalability and performance of edge federated learning are fundamentally constrained by synchronization bottlenecks. Clients operate under heterogeneous compute, time-varying communication conditions, and, in some settings, privacy constraints, yet synchronization is often still handled with fixed schedules. However, synchronization decisions are often made outside the client, even though the client directly observes local progress, resource state, and communication conditions. We present a client-side reinforcement learning synchronization framework in which each client decides during training whether to upload, download, synchronize bidirectionally, or defer communication. The framework places a lightweight scheduler alongside the local model and formulates synchronization as a resource-aware control problem driven by local learning and system state. We study this framework on two representative edge workloads, spatiotemporal traffic forecasting and image classification. Across both settings, adaptive client-side synchronization improves the accuracy-cost trade-off, reducing system cost in traffic forecasting while maintaining competitive cost and improving final accuracy in image classification. We also consider privacy-constrained settings, where synchronization must account for not only latency and energy but also privacy expenditure. Overall, our results show that synchronization in edge federated learning is better treated as an adaptive client-side control problem than only as a server-side coordination mechanism.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.14194: Vertical federated learning lets organizations train a shared model over features they hold separately, while one party keeps the labels private. The active label inference attack of Fu et al. [12] breaks this: a feature-holding party runs a modified optimizer, MaliciousSGD, that forces class structure into its embeddings and then recovers the labels with semi-supervised learning. Defenses that perturb the shared gradient fail, because the attack acts on the party's internal optimizer, not on the message it sends. We show the attack leaves a signal the server can read from the embeddings it already receives. The adversary's Fisher class-separability pulls away from the honest party's, and the gap is visible within a few epochs. A defense triggered by this signal acts on the adversary alone. Scaling its gradient down handles few-class tasks, and a norm non-expansive projection handles many-class tasks, with the Discriminative Coverage Ratio explaining why the projection rank must grow with the class count. The defense breaks the alignment between embedding clusters and labels rather than destroying the embedding. Across four seeds on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and CINIC-10, label inference falls below what honest training already leaks, at under two points of task-accuracy cost.
10.48550/arxiv.2610.11502: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong reasoning capabilities when fine-tuned with reinforcement learning (RL), particularly through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). However, existing GRPO methods assume centralized access to training data, which may not hold in practice due to privacy or regulatory constraints.
